title: Describe a neighbour who has helped you or your family.
prompts: who this neighbour is and how long you have known them
what kind of help they gave you
how you thanked them or returned the favour
and explain why this help meant so much to you.
angles: an elderly neighbour in your old flat
a family next door during an illness
a shopkeeper who lives in your building

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The person I want to talk about is ...
sentences: The neighbour I want to talk about is Rahim Uncle, who lives on the ground floor of our building in Mirpur.
We have known him for almost twelve years, ever since my family moved in.

steps.label: Background
steps.anchor: He is a retired bank officer, and the help he gave us was ...
sentences: He is a retired bank officer with a calm, dependable manner, and he has helped us in many small ways.
The biggest favour came when my father was hospitalised with dengue three years ago.
Rahim Uncle drove us to the hospital at midnight, waited with my mother for hours, and even arranged blood donors through his old contacts.

steps.label: What happened
steps.anchor: As for how we thanked him, ...
sentences: After my father recovered, we invited him for a proper dinner, and my mother cooked his favourite beef bhuna.
Since then we try to reciprocate whenever we can. I collect his medicine, and during Eid we send him a big tray of food.

steps.label: Why it mattered
steps.anchor: The reason it meant so much is that ...
sentences: It meant so much because we have no relatives in Dhaka, so we felt quite alone that night.
He did not have to go out of his way, yet he treated our problem as his own.
That showed me kindness does not depend on blood relations.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: So, he is more like a grandfather than a neighbour to me, and I hope I can help others the same way one day.

part3.q: Why do neighbours seem less close to each other in cities than in villages?
part3.a: I think it mainly comes down to lifestyle and space. In villages, people share fields, ponds and festivals, so they depend on each other daily. In a Dhaka apartment block, everyone leaves early for work, returns tired, and closes the door, so there are few chances to even talk.

part3.q: How has technology changed the way neighbours communicate?
part3.a: It has made contact quicker but also more shallow. Many buildings now have a Facebook or WhatsApp group where residents share notices about water supply or power cuts. That is useful, but people sometimes chat there for months without ever greeting each other on the stairs.

part3.q: Should people be expected to help neighbours they hardly know?
part3.a: I believe basic help should be expected, especially in emergencies. If someone's child is ill or a fire breaks out, waiting to become friends first would be absurd. However, I do not think anyone should feel forced to do big favours like lending large sums of money.

part3.q: What can local communities do to build stronger relationships between residents?
part3.a: Regular shared activities work best. A building could organise an iftar gathering during Ramadan or a small cultural evening, which gets families talking naturally. Clean-up days or a neighbourhood cricket match for children also help, because people bond while working or playing together.

phrases.m: people who know and support each other

title: Describe a teacher who made a difficult subject easy for you.
prompts: who the teacher was and what subject they taught
what methods they used in class
how your understanding of the subject changed
and explain why their way of teaching worked so well for you.
angles: a maths teacher in secondary school
an English teacher at a coaching centre

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The teacher I have in mind is ...
sentences: I would like to talk about Mr Karim, who taught me higher maths in Class Ten at my school in Chattogram.
Before his classes, maths was honestly my weakest and most dreaded subject.

steps.label: Teaching methods
steps.anchor: In class he used a few simple methods, ...
sentences: He never rushed through the textbook. Instead, he broke every complex idea into small steps and drew diagrams on the board until we could see the logic.
For trigonometry, he took us outside and measured the height of the school flagpole using shadows. Suddenly, those formulas felt real.
He also gave us a short quiz every Saturday, so mistakes were caught early.

steps.label: Change in understanding
steps.anchor: My understanding changed quite a lot, because ...
sentences: Within three months I stopped memorising formulas and began to understand where they came from.
My marks rose from around forty percent to almost ninety, and I even started solving extra problems for fun.

steps.label: Why it worked
steps.anchor: I think his style worked for me because ...
sentences: It worked because he was patient and approachable, and he never made anyone feel stupid for asking questions.
I tend to learn by seeing and doing, and his practical examples matched that perfectly.
He sparked an interest that stayed with me, since I later chose engineering.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: All in all, he showed me that no subject is truly difficult, only badly explained.

part3.q: What qualities make someone a good teacher?
part3.a: In my view, patience and clear communication matter most. A good teacher must understand the subject deeply enough to explain it in simple words. Also, genuine care for students is vital, because pupils work harder for someone they trust.

part3.q: Is private tuition necessary for students to do well in exams?
part3.a: I do not think it is truly necessary, but in Bangladesh it has become almost unavoidable. Classes are large, so teachers cannot give individual attention, and parents turn to tutors to fill the gap. The real problem is that it creates extra cost and pressure, which poorer families struggle with.

part3.q: How might online learning change the role of teachers in the future?
part3.a: I think teachers will become guides rather than just lecturers. Recorded lessons and AI tools can deliver basic content, so classroom time can be used for discussion and problem solving. Still, learners need human encouragement, so teachers will remain essential.

part3.q: Do you think teachers are respected enough in society today?
part3.a: Sadly, I feel respect has declined, particularly compared with my parents' generation. Teachers are often poorly paid, and some students treat them like service providers. If society valued them more, through better salaries and public recognition, the quality of education would improve.

phrases.m: explain hard things in simple parts
calm and easy to talk to

title: Describe a shopkeeper or street vendor in your area whom you know well.
prompts: who this person is and what they sell
how you first started buying from them
what you usually talk about when you meet
and explain why you keep going back to this person.
angles: a tea stall owner near your university
a vegetable seller in the local bazaar

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: Someone I know well in my area is ...
sentences: The person I would like to describe is Salam Bhai, who runs a small tea and snack stall at the corner of my street in Khulna.
He sells milk tea, singara and biscuits, and he has been there for more than twenty years.

steps.label: Background
steps.anchor: I first started buying from him ...
sentences: I first started going there in my first year of college, when my friends took me for an evening cha.
Since then I have become a regular customer, and now he prepares my tea with less sugar without even asking.

steps.label: What we talk about
steps.anchor: When we meet, we usually talk about ...
sentences: We chat about cricket, the price of rice, and the latest local gossip.
He often asks about my exams and shares stories about his own village. Sometimes he lets me pay at the end of the month when I run short of cash.
Over time we have built up a real rapport.

steps.label: Why I go back
steps.anchor: The reason I keep going back is that ...
sentences: The tea is good, but that is not the main reason. I keep going back because he treats everyone warmly, whether they are rich or poor.
In a city that often feels impersonal, that small human connection makes me feel I belong.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: So, for me his stall is not just a shop but a little part of my daily routine.

part3.q: Why do some people prefer small local shops to supermarkets?
part3.a: Mostly because of the personal touch. A local shopkeeper knows what you like, offers credit when needed, and lets you bargain. Many people also feel the goods, especially vegetables and fish, are fresher than in a big store.

part3.q: How has online shopping affected small traders?
part3.a: It has hit many of them quite hard. Customers compare prices on apps like Daraz and often find cheaper deals with home delivery. Small shops, particularly those selling clothes or electronics, have lost sales, although grocery shops have held up better.

part3.q: Do you think bargaining is a good way to buy things?
part3.a: It can be, if both sides are fair. In traditional markets it is part of the culture and lets buyers feel they got a good deal. But it can be stressful and unfair for people who are poor at negotiating, so fixed prices are better for essentials.

part3.q: What could be done to support small businesses in a city?
part3.a: Authorities could offer low-interest loans and simple licensing so small traders can grow. Training them to use mobile payments and social media would also help them compete. Finally, consumers can choose to spend part of their money locally, which keeps the neighbourhood economy alive.

phrases.m: someone who buys often from one place
shop owned and run by a family

title: Describe an older person who has told you interesting stories about the past.
prompts: who this person is and how you are connected to them
what kinds of stories they usually tell
where and when you listen to these stories
and explain what you have learned from hearing them.

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The person I want to describe is ...
sentences: I would like to talk about my grandfather, Dada, who is eighty-one and lives with us in Rajshahi.
He is my father's father, and he has always been the family storyteller.

steps.label: The stories
steps.anchor: The stories he tells are mostly about ...
sentences: Most of his stories are about his childhood in a village near the Padma, long before electricity arrived.
He describes walking miles to school barefoot, fishing with his cousins, and the fear and hope of 1971.
He tells them with such detail that I can almost see the paddy fields and hear the boats.

steps.label: When we listen
sentences: We usually sit on the veranda after Asr prayer, with tea and muri, when the heat has faded.
On Friday afternoons, when I am free from university, I sometimes record his stories on my phone so they are not lost.

steps.label: What I learned
steps.anchor: What I have learned is that ...
sentences: From him I have learned that people once lived with far fewer comforts but a lot more patience.
His first-hand experience of hardship makes me less likely to complain about small problems.
I also realised how quickly traditions disappear unless someone passes them down.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: In short, his stories are a living history book, and I feel lucky to be able to hear them.

part3.q: Why do young people today spend less time with older generations?
part3.a: Mainly because of busy schedules and technology. Many young people move to cities for study or work, so they see grandparents only during Eid. Even when they are at home, phones and streaming often take priority over conversation.

part3.q: What can older people teach the young that books cannot?
part3.a: They offer lived experience, which is full of context and emotion. A book may describe a famine or a war, but a person who survived it can explain how it felt and what they would do differently. They can also pass on practical skills and values, like patience and respect, through example.

part3.q: How important is it to record oral history before it is lost?
part3.a: I think it is very important, because many events are only remembered by the elderly. Once they pass away, those details disappear forever. Projects that record freedom fighters' memories, for example, give future generations a more human picture of history than official textbooks.

part3.q: Do you think the elderly are cared for well in your society?
part3.a: Traditionally, yes, since most elderly people live with their children, which is a strength of our culture. However, this is changing as families become smaller and more mobile. We now see more old people living alone, and the government and communities need to provide better healthcare and support.

phrases.m: hand customs to the next generation
difference between old and young views
history told by speaking, not writing

title: Describe a person in your community who works to help others.
prompts: who this person is and what they do
how they became involved in this work
how people in the community respond to them
and explain why you think their work is important.
angles: a doctor who gives free treatment
a youth volunteer running a food drive
a teacher who tutors poor children for free

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The person I have in mind is ...
sentences: The person I want to describe is Apa Shirin, a woman in our neighbourhood in Sylhet who runs a free evening school for street children.
She is about forty and works as a primary school teacher during the day.

steps.label: How she started
steps.anchor: She got involved in this work when ...
sentences: She told me it began about seven years ago, when she saw two children selling flowers near a traffic signal instead of attending school.
She started by teaching them letters on her own veranda, and gradually word spread.
Now around thirty children come every evening, and local shopkeepers donate notebooks and pencils.

steps.label: Community response
sentences: Honestly, the response has been very warm. Some neighbours give money each month, and a few college students volunteer to teach English and maths.
Of course, a handful of people complained about the noise at first, but they came round once they saw the children's progress.

steps.label: Why it matters
steps.anchor: I think her work is important because ...
sentences: I think her work matters because education is the best way for these kids to escape poverty.
She is truly selfless, since she receives no salary for it and sacrifices her own free time.
Her example makes ordinary people like me feel we can also make a real difference.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: So, she proves that you do not need money or power to give back to society, only commitment.

part3.q: Why are some people willing to volunteer while others are not?
part3.a: I think it depends on upbringing and free time. People raised in families that value service often feel it is natural to help. Others are simply too busy earning a living, so volunteering feels like a luxury to them.

part3.q: Should helping the needy be the government's job or individuals' responsibility?
part3.a: I believe it must be a shared effort. Governments have the resources and authority to run welfare schemes, health care and education on a large scale. But individuals and charities can reach people the system misses, and they often respond faster in emergencies like floods.

part3.q: How can young people be encouraged to take part in community work?
part3.a: Schools could make small service projects part of the curriculum, such as tree planting or cleaning drives. Young people also respond to recognition, so certificates or credit on a CV could motivate them. Seeing friends participate matters too, because they tend to follow their peers.

part3.q: Does social media help or harm charitable causes?
part3.a: On balance, I think it helps. A single viral post can raise money for a patient's surgery within hours, which was impossible before. The downside is fake appeals and people who share a post to feel good without actually donating, so verification is crucial.

phrases.m: help the community that helped you

title: Describe a friend from your past with whom you have lost touch.
prompts: who this friend was and how you met
what you used to do together
why you are no longer in contact
and explain how you feel about the friendship now.
angles: a childhood friend from your village
a school friend who moved abroad

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The friend I want to talk about is ...
sentences: I would like to talk about Tanvir, a childhood friend from my primary school days in Comilla.
We met on the first day of Class Three, when he shared his tiffin with me because I had forgotten mine.

steps.label: What we did together
steps.anchor: We used to spend our time ...
sentences: For about six years we were inseparable. We flew kites on the school roof, played cricket with a taped tennis ball, and cycled to the river after exams.
His mother often cooked khichuri for us on rainy days, and I still remember that smell.

steps.label: Why we lost touch
sentences: After Class Eight, his father was transferred and the family moved to Dubai. We wrote a few messages at first, but then I changed my phone number and lost his contact.
With exams and new friends, we simply drifted apart, and nobody did anything wrong.

steps.label: How I feel now
sentences: Now I feel a mix of fondness and regret. I sometimes scroll through social media hoping to find him, but his name is quite common.
I would love to reconnect someday, because those years shaped who I am.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: Overall, he reminds me that some friendships last only a season, but the memories stay.

part3.q: Why do friendships often fade when people move to a new city or job?
part3.a: Because daily contact is what keeps friendships alive. Once you no longer share a classroom or workplace, you must make a deliberate effort to meet, and most of us are too busy. New surroundings also bring new people, and our priorities gradually shift.

part3.q: Is it easier to keep in touch with friends today than in the past?
part3.a: Technically, yes. We can video call someone in Canada for free, whereas my parents relied on letters that took weeks. But easy contact does not guarantee close contact, since many of us only like each other's photos and rarely have real conversations.

part3.q: Do you think online friendships are as meaningful as real-life ones?
part3.a: They can be, depending on the depth of the conversation. I know people who found supportive friends in online study groups, and those bonds are genuine. Still, I think face-to-face time adds something special, like shared experiences and body language, that screens cannot fully replace.

part3.q: How do friends influence people at different stages of life?
part3.a: In adolescence, friends strongly shape our habits, style and even career choices, because we want to fit in. In adulthood, the influence becomes more about emotional support and advice. Later in life, good friends can protect against loneliness, which is a big issue for elderly people.

title: Describe a person you know who is very good at managing money.
prompts: who this person is and how you know them
how they plan and spend their money
what habits you have noticed in them
and explain what you could learn from the way they handle money.
angles: an older sister who works in a bank
a father who runs a small business
a university friend who saves carefully

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The person who comes to mind is ...
sentences: The person I would like to describe is my older sister, Nusrat, who works as an accounts officer at a private bank in Dhaka.
She is twenty-eight, and everyone in the family turns to her for money advice.

steps.label: How she spends
steps.anchor: She plans and spends in a way that ...
sentences: Every month, as soon as her salary arrives, she moves a fixed portion into a savings account before spending anything.
She keeps a simple budget in a notebook, dividing her income into rent, food, family support and fun money.
She stays within her means, but she is not stingy. She happily buys gifts for us on special occasions.

steps.label: Her habits
steps.anchor: One habit I have noticed is that ...
sentences: One habit I admire is that she compares prices and waits for sales instead of buying on impulse.
She also keeps an emergency fund covering six months of expenses, which saved her when she briefly lost her job two years ago.
She never takes loans for luxuries, and she tracks every taka on a mobile app.

steps.label: What I could learn
steps.anchor: What I could learn from her is ...
sentences: I could learn discipline, because I tend to spend my pocket money in the first week.
If I copied her habit of paying myself first, I could build real savings before graduating.
Also, I would feel far less stressed about unexpected costs.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: In short, she is financially savvy, and I am slowly trying to follow her example.

part3.q: Should schools teach children how to manage money?
part3.a: Definitely. Most people only learn about budgeting after making mistakes, which can be costly. If schools taught simple ideas like saving, interest and the difference between needs and wants, students would make wiser decisions as adults.

part3.q: Why do some people find it hard to save?
part3.a: There are a few reasons. Some have low incomes, so after covering rent and food nothing is left. Others are tempted by advertising and social media, where it seems everyone is buying new phones and clothes. Without a clear goal, saving feels pointless.

part3.q: How has digital payment, such as mobile banking, changed spending habits?
part3.a: It has made spending much easier and faster. With bKash or Nagad, people can pay for anything in seconds, so they sometimes lose track of how much they spend. On the positive side, it keeps a record of every transaction, which helps those who want to monitor their budget.

part3.q: Do you think young people today are more careless with money than older generations?
part3.a: I would say they face more temptation rather than being more careless. Online shopping, food delivery and constant discounts make spending effortless. Older generations had fewer choices, so thrift came naturally, but many young people are also learning about investing and saving through the internet.

title: Describe a public figure from your country who has inspired young people.
prompts: who this person is and what they are known for
how they became well known
how young people have reacted to them
and explain why you think they are a good influence.

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: A public figure who inspires me is ...
sentences: The person I would like to talk about is Shakib Al Hasan, the cricketer, who is widely admired by young people across Bangladesh.
He is known as one of the greatest all-rounders in world cricket.

steps.label: How he became famous
sentences: He grew up in Magura, a small town, and joined a cricket academy as a teenager.
He made his debut for the national team in 2006, and over the years he topped international all-rounder rankings, which put Bangladesh firmly on the cricketing map.

steps.label: Young people's reaction
sentences: Young fans adore him. Boys on every street try to copy his batting style, and his posters hang in many tea stalls.
When Bangladesh wins a close match, thousands gather in the streets to celebrate, and he is often the hero of those stories.
Many teenagers say he is the reason they took up the sport.

steps.label: Why he is a good influence
steps.anchor: I believe he is a good influence because ...
sentences: I think he shows that someone from a small town can reach the top through hard work and discipline.
His comebacks after injuries also teach resilience.
Of course, he has made some controversial decisions off the field, so I admire his sporting side most, but young people can certainly draw inspiration from his determination.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: So, he has given young Bangladeshis the belief that they can compete with anyone in the world.

part3.q: What makes someone a good role model for the young?
part3.a: I think honesty and perseverance are the key qualities. A role model should work hard, admit mistakes and treat others with respect. Fame alone is not enough, because young people copy behaviour, not only achievements.

part3.q: Do celebrities have a responsibility to set a good example?
part3.a: Yes, I believe they do, since millions of fans watch their every move. When a famous person promotes a harmful product or behaves rudely, many young followers see it as acceptable. At the same time, they are human, so we should be reasonable about their private lives.

part3.q: Are sportspeople more influential than politicians among young people?
part3.a: In my experience, yes. Sportspeople achieve results that everyone can see, such as winning a match, so they feel more authentic. Many young people distrust politicians because they hear a lot of promises with little visible change.

part3.q: How has social media changed the way people become famous?
part3.a: It has made fame faster and more democratic. A student with a phone can post a funny or talented video and reach millions overnight, without needing a TV channel. The downside is that this fame can be shallow and short-lived, and it often rewards controversy over real talent.

phrases.m: be remembered for a long time

title: Describe a busy market you have been to.
prompts: where the market is and what is sold there
what the atmosphere is like
what you did or bought there
and explain how you felt about being in such a crowded place.
angles: New Market or Gulshan kitchen market
a village hat on market day

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The busy market I remember is ...
sentences: The market I want to describe is the Chawkbazar area in Old Dhaka, which I visited last Ramadan with my cousin.
It is famous for its iftar items, spices, and clothes, and it gets extremely crowded before Eid.

steps.label: The atmosphere
sentences: The atmosphere was electric. Sellers shouted out their prices, the smell of fried jilapi and haleem filled the air, and rickshaw bells rang constantly.
Stalls were packed side by side, with bright fabrics hanging above and heaps of dates and fruit below.
It was honestly a sensory overload.

steps.label: What I did
sentences: We went to buy iftar snacks and a few dates for my grandmother.
I haggled for a bag of beguni and ended up paying a fair price, which felt like a small victory.
After shopping, we ate piping hot kebab on a plastic stool beside the road, watching the crowd flow past.

steps.label: My feelings
sentences: To be honest, my feelings were mixed. At first I felt excited by all the energy, but after an hour I was sweaty, someone stepped on my foot, and I could barely hear my cousin speak.
Still, I would go again, because that chaos is a part of the city's character.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: Overall, it was exhausting but unforgettable, and I would recommend it to anyone who wants to feel the real Dhaka.

part3.q: Why do many people still prefer traditional markets to shopping malls?
part3.a: I think it is mainly about price and experience. Traditional markets offer fresher produce, lower prices and the chance to bargain. Many people also enjoy the lively atmosphere, which feels more authentic than an air-conditioned mall.

part3.q: How might markets in cities change in the next few decades?
part3.a: I expect them to become more organised and cleaner, with permanent covered buildings instead of roadside stalls. Digital payments will likely replace cash, and some vendors will take orders through phone apps. Even so, I think the traditional character will survive because people love it.

part3.q: Is it a good idea to limit street trading to keep roads clear?
part3.a: I think limits are necessary, as stalls on roads cause traffic jams and sometimes accidents. But banning vendors completely would hurt thousands of poor families. A fairer solution is to give them designated spaces and fixed hours.

part3.q: What can local authorities do to keep public markets clean and safe?
part3.a: They should provide enough bins and regular waste collection, because rotting vegetables create both smell and disease. Fire safety is another concern, so wiring and exits should be inspected regularly. Finally, fining people who litter, along with awareness campaigns, would improve behaviour.

title: Describe a quiet place where you go when you want to think or study.
prompts: where this place is and how you found it
what it looks like and how it sounds
what you usually do there
and explain why this place helps you concentrate.

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The place I go to think is ...
sentences: The place I want to describe is a small reading corner on the third floor of my university library in Dhaka.
I discovered it by accident during my first semester, when the main hall was too noisy before a quiz.

steps.label: The place
sentences: It is a narrow space by a large window, with a wooden desk and a view of a big rain tree.
It is very quiet, and the only sounds are the gentle hum of the fan, a page turning, and sometimes birds outside.
Few students know about it, so it is almost always empty.

steps.label: What I do there
steps.anchor: When I am there, I usually ...
sentences: I usually go in the afternoon with my laptop, a notebook and a flask of tea.
I revise for exams, plan my week, or just sit and think about decisions, like which courses to take.
If I feel stressed, I write my worries on paper, which helps clear my head.

steps.label: Why it helps
sentences: It helps because it is free from distractions. There is no television, no noisy tea stall, and the Wi-Fi is weak, which means I am not tempted to scroll.
The natural light and greenery also give me peace of mind, so I can focus for two hours straight.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: That small corner is my peaceful retreat, and I always leave it feeling calmer and more organised.

part3.q: Why do some people need silence to work while others do not?
part3.a: I think it depends on personality and habit. Some people are easily distracted by sound, so they need silence to focus on complex tasks. Others grew up in crowded homes and are used to noise, and some even find mild background sound, like a cafe, helpful.

part3.q: Is it difficult to find quiet places in modern cities?
part3.a: Yes, particularly in a city like Dhaka. Traffic, horns, construction and crowded buildings make silence rare. Parks are few and often busy, so many students end up studying at night when the city finally calms down.

part3.q: Should schools and universities provide more quiet study areas?
part3.a: Definitely. Many students live in small, shared rooms at home, where they cannot concentrate. Dedicated silent zones in libraries would give them a fair chance to study well. It need not be expensive, since even a few partitioned rooms with good lighting would make a difference.

part3.q: How does the environment affect a person's productivity?
part3.a: Quite a lot, I believe. Good lighting, fresh air and a tidy desk make it easier to stay alert, while clutter and noise drain energy. I have noticed myself that I finish tasks much faster in a clean, calm space than in a messy room.

phrases.m: a quiet place to escape to

title: Describe an old building in your city or town.
prompts: where the building is and what it looks like
how old it is and what it was used for
what condition it is in today
and explain whether you think it should be preserved.
angles: a colonial-era building in Old Dhaka
a mosque or temple in your town
a zamindar house or rest house

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The old building I want to talk about is ...
sentences: The old building I want to describe is Ahsan Manzil, the pink palace beside the Buriganga river in Old Dhaka.
It is a large two-storey structure with a huge central dome, wide staircases and long arched corridors.

steps.label: Background
steps.anchor: It was built in ... and originally used as ...
sentences: It was built in the nineteenth century as a residence for a local nawab family, and it also hosted important gatherings.
I first visited it on a school trip, and I still remember how cool the thick walls felt.

steps.label: Condition today
sentences: Today it is a museum, and the government has restored most of it, so the pink paint looks fresh and the rooms are well kept.
However, the area around it is crowded and noisy, and some outer walls are stained by pollution and damp.
I think the building has survived better than many others, which have simply fallen into disrepair.

steps.label: Why it matters
steps.anchor: In my opinion, it should be preserved because ...
sentences: I strongly believe it should be preserved, because it tells us how people lived before modern Dhaka took shape.
Once a building like this is demolished, no amount of money can bring it back.
It also attracts visitors, which gives local traders a little extra income.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: So that is why I feel proud of this place, and I hope future generations will get to walk through those same corridors.

part3.q: Why is it important to protect historic buildings?
part3.a: Historic buildings are physical evidence of our past, so losing them is like tearing pages out of a history book. They also give a city its character, which is why tourists travel to see them. In Dhaka, for example, many old mansions disappeared and the city feels more generic because of it.

part3.q: Who should pay for the preservation of old buildings: the government or private owners?
part3.a: I think the cost should be shared. Private owners often cannot afford expensive restoration, so the government should offer grants or tax relief. On the other hand, owners who benefit from renting a heritage property should contribute too. A good example is a partnership where a company restores a house and then runs a cafe inside it.

part3.q: Should old buildings be replaced when cities need more housing?
part3.a: It depends on the building. If a structure is unsafe and has no real historic value, replacing it makes sense, especially in a crowded city like Dhaka. But a landmark should stay, and developers can build upwards in other areas instead. Balance is the key here.

part3.q: How can heritage sites be made interesting for young people?
part3.a: Sites need to be interactive, not just a row of dusty displays. Things like augmented reality tours, photography contests and short storytelling videos would appeal to teenagers. Schools could also run regular visits with a quiz or treasure hunt, so students enjoy learning instead of feeling forced.

title: Describe a village or rural area you have visited.

what the surroundings were like
what people did there in daily life
and explain how it was different from the place where you live.

steps.label: Opening

sentences: The village I want to talk about is my grandparents' home in Barishal, which I visited last winter with my parents and my younger brother.
It is about six hours from Dhaka by road and ferry, so the journey was part of the fun.

steps.label: The surroundings
steps.anchor: What struck me most was the scenery ...
sentences: What struck me most was the scenery: green paddy fields stretched in every direction, and narrow canals ran between small clusters of tin-roofed houses.
In the evening, the sky turned orange and you could hear nothing but birds and the occasional boat engine.

steps.label: Daily life
sentences: People there start their day very early. Farmers head to the fields at dawn, women dry rice or tend vegetable gardens, and children walk to the local school along the dirt paths.
In the afternoon, the men usually gather at the tea stall, chatting and sharing news.

steps.label: How it differed
sentences: Compared with Dhaka, it felt like another world. There was no traffic jam, no smoke, and the pace of life was so slow that nobody seemed in a hurry.
On the other hand, the internet was weak and there were few facilities like hospitals nearby.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: Overall, I came back feeling refreshed, and I would love to spend more time there.

part3.q: Why are so many people moving from villages to cities?
part3.a: Mainly because of jobs. Cities offer factories, offices and better wages, while farming income is unstable. People also move for education and healthcare. In Bangladesh, a lot of young men leave their villages for garment work in Dhaka or Gazipur.

part3.q: What are the advantages of living in the countryside?
part3.a: The biggest advantage is the peaceful, healthy environment. The air is cleaner, food is fresher, and the cost of living is lower. People also know their neighbours well, so there is a strong sense of community. I think that is hard to find in a crowded city.

part3.q: How could rural areas be made more attractive to young people?
part3.a: Better infrastructure would help a lot, such as reliable electricity, fast internet and good roads. Local governments could also set up small industries or training centres, so young people do not have to leave to find work. Online freelancing is a good example, since it can be done from a village.

part3.q: Do you think tourism helps or harms small rural communities?
part3.a: I think it can do both. It brings income through homestays, guides and local food stalls, which is a real benefit. However, too many visitors may create litter and change local traditions. So tourism needs to be limited and managed with the villagers' own involvement.

title: Describe a place where you had to wait for a long time.
prompts: where the place was and why you were there
how long you waited
what you did while waiting
and explain how you felt about the experience.

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: A time I had to wait for ages was ...
sentences: A time I had to wait for ages was at the passport office in Agargaon, when I went to submit my application last year.
I had heard it would be busy, but I did not expect what I saw.

steps.label: Background
sentences: I was there because I needed a passport for my IELTS test registration and then a future study plan abroad.
I arrived at seven in the morning to avoid the rush, yet there was already a long queue winding around the building.
In total, I waited almost five hours before someone finally called my number.

steps.label: What I did
sentences: To pass the time, I first scrolled through my phone, but the battery was nearly dead by ten o'clock.
So I started chatting with the man next to me, who was applying for a work visa, and we shared snacks and stories.
Later I reviewed some vocabulary on my notes app, which at least felt productive.

steps.label: How I felt
sentences: Honestly, I felt frustrated at first, because I was losing a whole morning and had skipped class.
But as time passed, I simply ran out of patience and then accepted it.
When my turn finally came, the process took only ten minutes, which felt ironic.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: In the end, I learned to carry a book and a power bank whenever I go to public offices.

part3.q: Why do people find waiting so frustrating?
part3.a: Because time feels valuable, and waiting makes us feel we have no control over it. When there is no information about how long it will take, people become anxious. I think that is why a delayed bus is more annoying when there is no announcement.

part3.q: Which public services in your country have the longest queues, and why?
part3.a: Hospitals, bank counters and government offices are probably the worst. There are simply too many people for the number of staff, and many processes are still done on paper. In Bangladesh, for instance, getting a birth certificate often takes several visits.

part3.q: Can technology help reduce waiting times?
part3.a: Definitely. Online booking and digital token systems mean people can arrive when it is their turn, instead of queuing for hours. Some hospitals already let patients book through apps. However, this only works if everyone, including older people, knows how to use it.

part3.q: Do you think people are less patient now than in the past?
part3.a: I would say yes. We are used to instant results, like fast delivery and instant messaging, so waiting feels unnatural. My grandfather can sit calmly for hours, but I get restless in a few minutes. Smartphones may help us pass time, but they also shorten our attention span.

title: Describe a river, lake or waterside place you have seen.
prompts: where the water is and when you went there
what the view was like
what people were doing around it
and explain why this place stayed in your memory.

steps.label: Opening

sentences: The place I would like to describe is Kaptai Lake in Rangamati, which I visited with my cousins during the winter holidays two years ago.

steps.label: The view
sentences: The view was breathtaking. The water was perfectly calm, and green hills rose all around it, with tiny islands scattered across the surface.
As the sun went down, the whole lake turned golden, and the reflections made it look like a painting.
There was a soothing atmosphere, with only the gentle sound of engines in the distance.

steps.label: What people did
sentences: Around the shore, local fishermen were pulling in their nets, and children were jumping into the shallows and laughing.

steps.label: Why I remember it

sentences: It stayed in my memory because it was the first time I felt truly calm in months. I had been stressed with exams, and the quiet scenery cleared my mind.
Also, my cousins and I talked more that day than we had in years.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: So whenever I feel overwhelmed, I close my eyes and picture that lake.

part3.q: Why do people feel relaxed near water?
part3.a: I think the sound and movement of water have a natural calming effect on the mind. It is also usually open and green nearby, which gives a sense of space. Many people say they sleep better after a day by a river or lake.

part3.q: What problems do rivers and lakes face in your country?
part3.a: Pollution is the biggest one. Factories release untreated waste, and households throw rubbish into the water. The Buriganga in Dhaka is a sad example. Encroachment is another issue, because land grabbers fill in parts of rivers to build on them.

part3.q: Who should be responsible for keeping waterways clean?
part3.a: I think it is a shared responsibility. The government must enforce laws and punish factories that pollute, but ordinary people should also stop dumping waste. Local communities can help by organising clean-up drives, and schools can teach children to respect rivers from an early age.

part3.q: How might climate change affect places near water in the future?
part3.a: Rising sea levels and stronger floods could damage homes and farmland, especially in coastal Bangladesh. Salt water may also enter freshwater sources. On the other hand, dry seasons could shrink lakes. So countries need to plan ahead with embankments and early warning systems.

title: Describe a place in your area that you would like to see improved.

what problems it has at the moment
what changes you would like to see

steps.label: Opening

steps.label: Current problems

steps.label: Proposed changes
sentences: If I could change it, I would first level the ground and add grass and a jogging track around the edge.
I would also install solar street lights, some benches and bins, and repaint the play equipment.

steps.label: Benefit to locals
sentences: These changes would help local people in many ways. Children would have a safe place to play, and parents would feel comfortable letting them go outside.

steps.label: Wrap-up

part3.q: Who should decide how public spaces are developed?
part3.a: I believe it should be a joint decision. City authorities and planners have technical knowledge, but residents know their own needs best. So there should be public meetings or surveys before any project begins. Otherwise, money can be wasted on things nobody actually wants.

part3.q: Do cities in your country have enough green areas?
part3.a: Not at all, especially in places like Dhaka. Buildings have taken over almost every empty plot, and parks are few and often crowded. As a result, children have nowhere to play and air quality suffers. More rooftop gardens and small pocket parks could partly solve this.

part3.q: How can residents be involved in improving their neighbourhoods?
part3.a: They can join local committees, take part in clean-up days or report problems to the city corporation through hotlines and apps. Some communities also raise small funds to plant trees. When people feel ownership of a place, they look after it much better.

part3.q: Is it better to spend public money on new projects or on repairing existing ones?
part3.a: I think maintenance should come first. New projects like flyovers are impressive, but if old roads and drains are neglected, the city keeps deteriorating. Repairs are usually cheaper and benefit people immediately. That said, new projects are necessary when the population outgrows existing facilities.

title: Describe a public place near your home where people like to gather.

sentences: So I would say it is the heart of our neighbourhood.

part3.q: Why are public gathering places important in a community?
part3.a: They give people a space to meet and mix with others from different backgrounds. That builds trust and a sense of belonging. They also support health, because people can exercise or simply relax. In a crowded city, such places act like the lungs of a neighbourhood.

part3.q: Have people started to use public spaces less because of the internet?
part3.a: To some extent, yes. Many young people prefer chatting online or gaming at home. However, I do not think public spaces will lose their value, because nothing replaces face-to-face contact. In fact, parks near me are as busy as before, particularly in the evenings.

part3.q: How can cities make public places safe for women and children?
part3.a: Good lighting, CCTV cameras and regular patrols are the basics. Clear paths without hidden corners also help. Authorities should act strictly against harassment, and have visible helplines. Designing separate play zones for children can keep them away from traffic and strangers.

part3.q: Should public parks and playgrounds be free for everyone?
part3.a: I think so, or at least entry should be very cheap. Public spaces belong to everyone, and charging high fees would exclude poorer families. Maintenance costs can be covered through taxes or small charges for special events. A free park benefits health and community life, so it is a good investment.

title: Describe an old object in your home that has been kept in your family for many years.

steps.label: Origin
sentences: It originally belonged to my great-grandmother, who brought it with her when she moved to her husband's village after her wedding.
She used it to light the house in the evenings before electricity reached the area, and later my grandmother kept it in her prayer corner.

steps.label: Care and use
sentences: These days, we do not use it for lighting, but we take it out during special occasions, like Eid and family gatherings, and place it near the entrance.

steps.label: Why it matters

sentences: It is important to my family because it connects us to people we never met, or can barely remember.
Every time I look at it, I picture my great-grandmother's hands holding it.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: So I hope it will be passed down to my children one day.

part3.q: Why do some families keep old objects for generations?
part3.a: Because those objects carry memories and a sense of identity. Holding something that an ancestor used makes the past feel real. Families also feel a duty to preserve what earlier generations worked hard to own. In Bangladesh, people often keep jewellery, utensils or old books for exactly this reason.

part3.q: Do young people value traditional items as much as older people do?
part3.a: Generally not as much. Younger people grow up with modern, disposable products and may see old things as outdated. However, I think that changes with age, once they start to appreciate their roots. Some teenagers now like vintage styles, so interest is slowly coming back.

part3.q: Should museums collect everyday objects from ordinary households?
part3.a: Yes, I think so. Museums usually display items from kings and wealthy people, but ordinary objects show how most people really lived. A cooking pot or school slate can tell us about daily routines and technology. If those things are not collected, that history will be lost.

part3.q: How has the way people treat their possessions changed over time?
part3.a: In the past, people repaired and reused things for years, as they were expensive. Now mass production makes goods cheap, so we tend to replace them quickly. This habit creates a lot of waste. Fortunately, some people are returning to repairing and recycling, because they care about the environment.

part3.q: Why do some people prefer buying second-hand goods?
part3.a: Mostly because it saves money. A pre-owned item can cost half the price of a new one, and quality is often still good. Some people also care about the environment, and reusing things reduces waste. Others simply like unique items, such as vintage furniture or old books.

part3.q: Is it better to repair old things or replace them with new ones?
part3.a: I think repairing is usually better, if the cost is reasonable. It saves money and reduces waste. However, with some electronics, repair can cost almost as much as a new product, or spare parts are not available. In that case, replacing is more sensible. My father repaired our fan three times, and it still works.

part3.q: How has online shopping changed the market for used items?
part3.a: It has made it much easier. Sellers can post photos on Facebook groups or sites like Bikroy and reach thousands of buyers instantly. Buyers can compare prices without going from shop to shop. On the other hand, there is more risk of scams, so people need to be careful and meet in person.

part3.q: Do you think people today buy more than they really need?
part3.a: Yes, I do. Advertising and social media make us feel we need the latest phone or fashion, even when our current one works fine. Easy credit and discounts encourage impulse buying as well. As a result, many homes are filled with things that are hardly ever used.

It has become a real household essential.

sentences: I honestly cannot imagine our kitchen without it.

part3.q: How have kitchen appliances changed the way families live?
part3.a: They have made cooking faster and less tiring, which gives families more free time. In the past, women often spent most of the day in the kitchen. Now appliances like rice cookers and fridges let everyone share household work more easily. People can also store food for days, so shopping is less frequent.

part3.q: Are modern gadgets making people less skilled at cooking?
part3.a: In some ways, yes. Many young people rely on microwaves and ready-made mixes, so they never learn basic techniques. However, gadgets can also encourage people to try new recipes. I think it depends on the person. Those who enjoy cooking will learn the skills anyway.

part3.q: Who should do household chores in a family, and why?
part3.a: Everyone who lives in the house should share them, in my opinion. It is unfair to expect one person, usually the mother, to do everything. Children can set the table or wash their own plates, and fathers can cook or clean. Sharing chores also teaches responsibility and teamwork.

part3.q: Do you think technology will fully automate housework in the future?
part3.a: Probably not fully, but a large part. Robot vacuum cleaners and smart ovens already exist, and they will get cheaper. part3.q: Why are traditional clothes still worn on special occasions?

part3.q: Is fashion in your country influenced too much by foreign trends?

part3.q: Should schools or workplaces require a particular style of dress?
part3.a: I think a simple dress code is reasonable, because uniforms create equality and a sense of discipline in schools. At work, neat clothing gives a professional impression. But the rules should not be too strict, and should respect people's culture and comfort, especially in hot weather.

part3.q: Will traditional clothing survive as lifestyles keep modernising?

part3.q: Why do people become so upset when they lose small personal items?

part3.q: Can technology, such as tracking apps, solve the problem of lost belongings?

title: Describe a notebook, diary or book that you have kept for a long time.

The cover is faded now, and many pages are dog-eared because I carried it in my school bag everywhere.

steps.label: What it contains
sentences: Inside, there are silly drawings, exam worries, jokes my friends made, and even a few awkward poems about the monsoon.
Some entries are painful to read because my handwriting is terrible and my opinions were so dramatic.

steps.label: Why it matters
steps.anchor: The reason I cannot let go is ...
sentences: I look at it only once or twice a year, usually on a quiet Friday afternoon. I flip through it, laugh a little, and sometimes feel nostalgic.
My grandmother passed away two years ago, so her gift has become a keepsake that I could never throw away.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: It shows me how much I have changed, and that is priceless. One day I hope to show it to my own children, as a reminder that small habits can build something precious.

part3.q: Do you think people will still keep paper books and notes in the future?
part3.a: I believe paper will survive, although in smaller amounts. Many people enjoy the feel and smell of a real book, and handwritten notes feel more personal. Even in a digital age, you still see students buying notebooks for the start of every term.

part3.q: Why do some people prefer writing by hand to typing?
part3.a: Writing by hand slows you down, so you think more carefully and remember better. Several studies suggest that students who take handwritten notes understand lectures more deeply. Personally, I also find it calming, because there are no notifications to distract me.

part3.q: Is keeping a diary a useful habit for young people?
part3.a: Yes, I think so, as long as it is not forced. A diary helps teenagers sort out their emotions and track their progress. For example, a classmate of mine used hers to manage exam stress, and it clearly helped her stay calm.

part3.q: How might digital storage change the way we remember our past?
part3.a: Digital storage makes remembering easier but also messier. We will have thousands of photos and messages, but we may never look at them. On the other hand, nothing will be lost in a fire or flood, so future generations may know their ancestors better than we do.

title: Describe a piece of furniture at home that you find very comfortable or useful.
prompts: what it is and where it is placed
what it is made of and how it looks
how you and your family use it
and explain why it matters to you

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The piece of furniture I am fond of is ...
sentences: The piece of furniture I find most useful is the old wooden sofa in our living room in Chattogram.
It sits against the wall facing the window, so it catches the evening breeze.

steps.label: Description
sentences: It is made of solid teak, which is why it is so sturdy, and my father had green cushions made for it a few years ago. The armrests are a little scratched, but the dark polished wood still looks elegant.
It is certainly not fashionable, yet it has plenty of character.

steps.label: How we use it
sentences: Everyone uses it differently. My father reads the newspaper there each morning, my mother naps on it after lunch, and I often stretch out with my laptop.
When guests visit, it turns into extra seating, and on Eid it somehow fits six people.

steps.label: Why it matters
sentences: For me, it is the heart of our home. Most of our conversations, arguments and tea breaks happen around it.
I have also done my best studying there, because it is comfortable without being so soft that I fall asleep.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: It has lasted over twenty years, and I would love to have it in my own home one day.

part3.q: How important is a comfortable home to a person's well-being?
part3.a: It is very important, because a home is where people recover from the stress of work or study. If the space is cramped, noisy or uncomfortable, it affects sleep and mood. A comfortable home does not need to be expensive, just clean and peaceful.

part3.q: Why do many people in cities live in small flats with little furniture?
part3.a: Mainly because of cost and space. Rents in cities like Dhaka are extremely high, so families rent small flats and keep only essential items. Many also choose folding or multi-purpose furniture, like beds with storage, simply to save room.

part3.q: Would you rather buy cheap furniture often or expensive furniture once?
part3.a: I would go for expensive, durable furniture bought once. Cheap pieces tend to break within a couple of years, so you spend more in the long run. My uncle bought a solid wood wardrobe twenty years ago and it still looks new.

part3.q: How might homes and furniture look different in fifty years?
part3.a: I think homes will be smaller and smarter. Furniture may be modular, so a desk can fold into a wall at night. With more people working remotely, I also expect tables and chairs to be designed for comfort and good posture.

title: Describe something handmade that someone made for you.
prompts: what it is and who made it
how long it probably took to make
what it is used for
and explain why it is special to you
angles: a painted card or a clay gift

steps.label: Opening
sentences: I would like to talk about a kantha quilt that my grandmother stitched for me.
It is a handmade blanket made from old saris, with colourful flowers and birds sewn along the border.

steps.label: Who made it
sentences: She made it when I left home for university in Dhaka, and I think it took her nearly three months, working a little every afternoon.
Her eyes are weak now, so she had to sew very slowly, and she even redid a few sections to get them right.

steps.label: Time and use
sentences: I use it every night, especially in winter when the hostel room gets cold. During the day, I fold it neatly on my bed, and it makes the room feel like home.
Friends often ask where I bought it, and they are surprised when I say nobody could buy one like it.

steps.label: Why it is special
sentences: It is special because it is one of a kind. Every stitch is a reminder of the time and patience she put into it.
Whenever I feel homesick or stressed, I wrap myself in it and instantly feel looked after.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: I know that a shop could never sell me this kind of comfort, so I plan to keep it for the rest of my life.

part3.q: Why are handmade items often more valued than factory-made ones?
part3.a: Because they carry a personal touch. You can see the effort and care in them, while factory items are identical. A handmade gift also shows that someone spent time thinking about you, and that makes people appreciate it more.

part3.q: Are traditional crafts disappearing in your country, and does it matter?
part3.a: To some extent, yes. Cheap machine-made products have replaced many items, and fewer young people want to learn skills like pottery or weaving. It matters because crafts are part of our identity, and once the knowledge disappears, it is hard to recover.

part3.q: Should the government support small craft businesses?
part3.a: Yes, I think they should. Small craft businesses, especially in villages, often lack funds and markets. The government could offer low-interest loans, training and help to sell abroad. Nakshi kantha is already famous overseas, so there is clear potential.

part3.q: Do you think a handmade gift is better than an expensive shop-bought one?
part3.a: For me, a handmade gift wins, as long as it is made with real care. A pricey gift can feel impersonal, while a hand-painted card or a knitted scarf shows effort. That said, the best gift depends on the person, and some people might prefer something practical.

phrases.m: slowly, one small step at a time
object passed down in a family

title: Describe a family gathering during a festival such as Eid or Pohela Boishakh.
prompts: when and where the gathering took place
who came and what you did together
what food or activities were part of it
and explain what made it memorable

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: One gathering I will never forget is ...
sentences: I would like to describe last Eid-ul-Fitr, when our whole extended family met at my grandparents' village house in Bogura.
We had not all been together for nearly three years, so everyone was excited.

steps.label: Setting and guests
sentences: Almost thirty relatives came, including uncles from Dhaka and cousins who now live abroad. The courtyard was crowded from morning till night.
After the Eid prayer, we visited neighbours, and the younger kids went around collecting salami.

steps.label: Food and activities
sentences: The kitchen was the busiest place. My aunts made semai, polao and a rich beef curry, and my grandmother insisted that everyone eat twice.
In the evening, we sat on the veranda, played carrom, and my uncle told old stories about his childhood.

steps.label: What made it memorable
sentences: It was memorable because of the festive atmosphere and the sense of belonging. Nobody was staring at their phones for once.
I also felt grateful watching my grandparents smile as they looked at three generations under one roof.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: Looking back, it reminded me that traditions matter, and I am determined to carry it on wherever I live.

part3.q: Why are family gatherings important in your culture?
part3.a: In our culture, family is the core of social life, and relatives often support each other financially and emotionally. Gatherings give everyone a chance to reconnect. They also teach children respect for elders and shared values.

part3.q: Have festivals become more commercial than they used to be?
part3.a: I think so, to a degree. Shops start Eid sales weeks ahead, and advertising pushes people to buy expensive clothes. Yet the spirit has not disappeared, because families still cook together and visit one another. The balance has just shifted towards spending.

part3.q: Do young people celebrate traditions differently from their grandparents?
part3.a: Yes, quite a lot. My grandparents like long, formal visits, whereas many young people prefer to celebrate with friends or post photos online. However, most youngsters still join the family meal, so the core tradition is alive, just in a modern form.

part3.q: How can people who live far from home stay connected to family celebrations?
part3.a: Video calls are the obvious answer, and they work well. Families can eat at the same time while chatting online. Sending small gifts or money, and cooking the same dish, also helps. It is never as good as being there, but it reduces homesickness.

phrases.m: meet family after a long gap
feeling of being part of a group

title: Describe a time when you were caught in heavy rain or a storm.
prompts: where you were and what you were doing
what the weather was like
what you did to deal with the situation
and explain how you felt afterwards
angles: a cyclone warning in a coastal town
a sudden storm on a journey

steps.label: Opening
sentences: I would like to describe an afternoon last July when I got caught in a torrential downpour in Dhaka.
It was meant to be an ordinary day, and I had no umbrella.

steps.label: Where I was
steps.anchor: I was on my way to ...
sentences: I was cycling home from a friend's house near Dhanmondi, thinking about dinner, when the sky suddenly turned almost black.
Within minutes, huge drops were hammering down, and the wind was strong enough to bend the roadside trees.

steps.label: What I did
sentences: The streets were already waterlogged, so I could not keep going. I pushed my bike to a small tea stall and took shelter under its tin roof with a few rickshaw pullers.
My phone was soaked, so I wrapped it in my shirt and waited.

steps.label: Weather detail
sentences: We chatted and drank hot tea for nearly an hour. Then the rain eased and I waded home through knee-deep water, laughing at how ridiculous I looked.
I was soaked to the skin, and my shoes were ruined.

steps.label: Afterwards
sentences: Afterwards I felt oddly cheerful, and a bit proud. It reminded me how small we are against nature, but also how kind strangers can be in a crisis.

part3.q: How does extreme weather affect daily life in your country?
part3.a: It affects us in many ways. Heavy rain floods roads and delays offices and schools, and cyclones in the south can destroy homes. In summer, heatwaves make outdoor work unbearable. People have learned to adapt, but poorer families suffer the most.

part3.q: Should people be more prepared for natural disasters?
part3.a: Absolutely. Bangladesh is one of the most disaster-prone countries, so being prepared saves lives. Cyclone shelters and early-warning systems have already reduced deaths. Households should also keep emergency kits, and schools should run regular drills.

part3.q: Do you think climate change is making weather more unpredictable?
part3.a: I think so. Seasons seem less predictable now, with rain arriving late or too heavily. Scientists link this to rising global temperatures, and farmers in my country say they can no longer rely on old patterns. It is a worrying trend.

part3.q: What can governments do to protect citizens during severe weather?
part3.a: Governments can invest in drainage, strong embankments and shelters. They should also send timely warnings by text message and radio. After a disaster, quick relief and rebuilding support matter too. Prevention is always cheaper than recovery.

title: Describe a time when you had to wait a long time for something.

where you waited and for how long
what you did while waiting
and explain how you felt about the experience
angles: an exam result or a train ticket

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: A time when I had to wait ages was ...
sentences: I would like to talk about the day I waited for my passport at a regional office in Dhaka.
I had an urgent university application, so I really needed it that week.

steps.label: What and where
sentences: I arrived at seven in the morning, thinking I would be done by lunch. Instead, the line was already outside the gate and the process dragged on until almost five in the evening.
That made it about ten hours, which is far longer than I expected.

steps.label: What I did
sentences: To kill time, I chatted with the people around me, scrolled through my phone until the battery died, and read a few pages of a novel.
I also made a friend, an engineer returning to Dubai, and we shared snacks while we waited for our numbers to be called.

steps.label: Feelings
sentences: At first I stayed positive, but by the afternoon I lost patience and felt exhausted and annoyed. I even considered leaving.
When my name was finally called, the relief was huge, and the process itself took five minutes.

steps.label: Wrap-up
steps.anchor: The lesson I took away was ...
sentences: Looking back, I learned to bring a charger and water to any office. More importantly, I realised that patience is a skill, and I practise it more now.

part3.q: Are people today less patient than in the past?
part3.a: I believe so. With instant messaging and fast delivery, we have become used to immediate results. When a video buffers for ten seconds, many of us feel irritated. Our grandparents were accustomed to waiting for letters for weeks.

part3.q: Why do some services involve long waiting times in your country?
part3.a: There are several reasons. Offices are often understaffed, and many procedures still depend on paper forms and manual checks. Population density adds to it, as too many people use the same service. As a result, queues form even for simple tasks.

part3.q: Can technology reduce the time people spend queuing?
part3.a: Yes, definitely. Online booking, digital tokens and mobile payments already save time, for example when buying train tickets. If government offices put forms online, people wouldn't need to stand in line for hours. The challenge is making it accessible to everyone.

part3.q: Is waiting ever a good thing, or is it always a waste of time?
part3.a: Sometimes it is positive. Waiting can teach patience, and a pause lets people think or talk. Good things, like a home-cooked meal or a degree, take time too. But when it is caused by poor management, it is simply a waste of time.

phrases.p: on the edge of my seat

title: Describe a day when you had to get up much earlier than usual.

what you did that morning
who was with you

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: A day I had to wake up unusually early was ...
sentences: I would like to describe a morning in February when I woke up at four o'clock to catch a bus to Sylhet.
I normally sleep until seven, so it felt like the middle of the night.

steps.label: Why I woke up early
sentences: My university had organised a one-day trip to the tea gardens, and the bus was leaving at five-thirty sharp.
I had a tight schedule, because I still needed to pack snacks and walk to the meeting point.

steps.label: The morning
steps.anchor: As soon as I got up, ...
sentences: I set the alarm on my phone and a backup on my brother's, but I still woke up bleary-eyed. I washed my face with cold water, grabbed a banana and rushed out in the dark.
The streets were silent, apart from a few bakers and a rickshaw puller drinking tea.

steps.label: Who was there
sentences: My roommate Rafi came with me, and we yawned all the way, laughing at how ridiculous we both looked. Most of the group fell asleep on the bus.

steps.label: Was it worthwhile?
sentences: It definitely turned out to be worthwhile. We reached the hills as the mist was lifting, and the green gardens glowed in the early light.
I realised that mornings can be beautiful, so now I try to rise at six once a week.

part3.q: Do you think being an early riser leads to a more successful life?
part3.a: Not necessarily. Many successful people get up early, but others work best at night. What matters is using your time well. Early rising can give a quiet start, though, and I find I focus much better before nine.

part3.q: How do people's sleep habits differ between city and village life?
part3.a: In villages, people follow the sun. Farmers get up at dawn and sleep soon after dinner. In cities, electricity and late-night work or study mean people stay up long and sleep late. Traffic also pushes many commuters to wake up early.

part3.q: Should schools and offices start later in the day?
part3.a: I think starting later would help, especially for teenagers. Their body clocks shift at that age, so they struggle with early mornings. Some countries have already tried a later school day and reported better results. Offices could offer flexible hours as well.

part3.q: What are the effects of lack of sleep on young people?
part3.a: Lack of sleep affects concentration, memory and mood. Students who stay up late for exams or social media often feel drained and perform worse. In the long term, it can harm their health. Schools should teach good sleep habits.

title: Describe an event you helped to organise at school, university or in your neighbourhood.

what your role was in organising it
what problems came up and how they were solved
and explain what you learned from the experience

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The event I helped with was ...
sentences: I would like to talk about an inter-department cultural programme that I helped organise at my university last year.
It was a one-day event for around four hundred students, with songs, dance and a small drama competition.

steps.label: The event
sentences: Our department wanted the freshers to feel welcome, so a group of ten of us formed a committee.
We planned everything from the guest list to the stage decoration over about a month.

steps.label: My role
sentences: I took charge of logistics, which meant booking the auditorium, arranging chairs and sound equipment, and coordinating the volunteers.
I made a checklist for each person, and I stayed up late a few times to print tickets and banners.

steps.label: Problems and solutions

Fortunately, the event ran smoothly and nobody in the audience noticed.

steps.label: What I learned
sentences: I learned that teamwork and clear communication matter more than perfect planning. I also learned to stay calm under pressure, a skill that has helped me in exams since.

part3.q: Why is it valuable for young people to take part in community activities?
part3.a: It teaches them responsibility and helps them make friends beyond the classroom. They also see how their efforts benefit others. In my country, many students focus only on exams, so community work balances that with real-life experience.

part3.q: What skills does a person need to organise a successful event?
part3.a: Mainly planning, leadership and communication. You also need patience to deal with people, and the ability to solve problems quickly, because something always goes wrong. Time management matters as well, especially when deadlines are close.

part3.q: Should students be given more responsibility for organising school events?
part3.a: I think so, with some guidance from teachers. When students lead, they gain confidence and creativity. But too much freedom can lead to mistakes, so a staff member should be there to support. A mix of independence and supervision works best.

part3.q: How do community events help bring people together?
part3.a: They give neighbours a reason to meet. In our area, a Friday cricket match or a Victory Day programme lets families who rarely talk spend time together. Shared activities build trust, and that makes the community safer and friendlier.

title: Describe a wedding you attended that you remember well.

what happened during the ceremony and celebration
what you wore and ate

steps.label: Opening

steps.label: Setting and ceremony
sentences: The celebration began with the holud, where relatives smeared turmeric paste on the bride and everyone sang and danced. The next day, the akhd ceremony took place, and the groom's family arrived in a long procession of decorated cars.
The hall was lavish, with flowers and bright lights everywhere.

steps.label: Clothes and food
sentences: I wore a deep green panjabi that my mother had picked out, and the women wore bright saris. The food was incredible: biryani, roast, borhani and a huge platter of sweets.

steps.label: Why I remember it
sentences: I remember it so clearly because Nadia cried when she said goodbye to her parents, and soon the whole room was emotional. Meanwhile my grandfather danced for the first time in years, and everyone clapped.
It showed me how a wedding unites the extended family.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: Overall, it was exhausting but wonderful, and I still watch the photos when I want to smile.

part3.q: Why do weddings in your country often involve so many guests?
part3.a: Because marriage is seen as a union of two families, not just two people. Relatives, neighbours and even colleagues are invited as a sign of respect. Inviting fewer guests might offend people, so the lists keep growing.

part3.q: Do you think families spend too much money on weddings?
part3.a: I think many families overspend. Some borrow money just to impress others, and then struggle with debt for years. A wedding should be joyful, not a financial burden. Spending on the couple's future, such as a house, is more sensible.

part3.q: How have wedding customs changed over the last few decades?
part3.a: They have become more flashy. Pre-wedding photoshoots and themed decorations were unknown to my parents. Yet core rituals, like holud and the wedding feast, remain. Also, couples now have more say in choosing their partner than earlier generations did.

part3.q: Is it better to have a simple wedding or a grand one?
part3.a: I lean towards a simple wedding. What matters is the commitment, not the show. A modest event also means less stress and more time with close people. However, I understand that for some families, a grand wedding is a source of pride and joy.

steps.label: Introduction

steps.label: Setting off
sentences: We were going to visit my grandparents for Eid, so the whole platform was packed with families carrying bags and sacks of gifts. The trip was supposed to take about seven hours, but the train was delayed, so it stretched to nearly ten.

steps.label: On the way
sentences: Once we got moving, I spent most of the time at the window. As the sun came up, the tea gardens appeared, rolling green hills covered in mist, and it was the most scenic stretch I have ever seen. My brother and I shared a packet of puffed rice and chatted with a stranger who gave us a tour of local snacks.

steps.label: Why I remember it
steps.anchor: Would I do it again? Honestly ...
sentences: It was tiring, of course, because the carriage was overcrowded and I barely slept. Still, the view and the strangers' kindness made the hardship feel worthwhile.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: I would happily make the same journey again, though I would book a proper seat in advance. Some trips are about the road, not just the destination.

part3.q: Why do many people still prefer travelling by road or train rather than by air?
part3.a: Mainly because it is cheaper and far more accessible. A bus ticket from Dhaka to Chattogram costs a fraction of a flight, and the terminal is usually close to where people live. Besides, many Bangladeshis carry heavy luggage or travel with elderly parents, and trains handle that much more easily than airlines.

part3.q: How can public transport in your country be improved?
part3.a: I think punctuality and safety are the first priorities. If trains actually ran on time and buses did not overtake dangerously, more people would trust them. We also need online ticketing that works reliably, because queuing at counters before Eid is exhausting, and extra coaches on the busiest routes would reduce overcrowding.

part3.q: Does travelling teach people things that classrooms cannot?
part3.a: Yes, I believe so. In a classroom you read about a place, but on the road you meet people whose lives are completely different from yours. My own train trip showed me how patient and generous strangers can be, which no textbook could teach me, and it also built my confidence in solving small problems on my own.

part3.q: How might long-distance travel change in the future?
part3.a: I expect faster and cleaner options to become common, such as high-speed rail and electric buses. Here in Bangladesh, the new bridges and the metro are already shortening journeys that once took a full day. However, I hope slow travel survives, because some people really value the experience of watching a country pass by.
