steps.label: Lesson learned
sentences: That experience taught me to adapt on the spot instead of sulking. These days I always keep a plan B, and I see changes as a chance to discover something better.

part3.q: Is it better to plan everything carefully or to be flexible?
part3.a: I think a mixture works best. Careful planning gives you direction, especially for exams or business, but life rarely follows a script. If you cling to the plan too tightly, you panic when something shifts, so I prefer a solid outline with room to adjust.

part3.q: Why do some people find sudden change stressful?
part3.a: Probably because they like control and predictability. When a routine breaks, they fear losing time, money or status. In Bangladesh, for example, a sudden strike can ruin a whole day of work, so people become anxious about anything that threatens their schedule.

part3.q: Can unexpected events ever turn out to be positive for a person?
part3.a: Definitely. Many people describe a job loss or a failed application as a blessing in disguise because it pushed them toward a better path. I know someone who missed a scholarship but started a small online business, which later became far more rewarding.

part3.q: Should schools teach young people how to cope with uncertainty?
part3.a: Yes, I think they should. Our education system focuses heavily on memorising answers, so students often struggle when a problem has no clear solution. Simple activities like group projects with changing conditions, or discussions about handling setbacks, would build resilience early.

title: Describe a game you used to play with other children in your neighbourhood when you were young.

steps.label: Who and where
sentences: I played with about eight neighbourhood kids, including my cousin and two boys from the corner shop. We met every day after Asr prayer, when the heat eased, and played until someone's mother called them in for dinner.

sentences: One afternoon, I tripped while escaping and scraped my knee badly, but I refused to quit. My friends laughed, then helped me finish the round, and I still have a tiny scar.

steps.label: Why it stays with me
steps.anchor: I remember it so well because ...
sentences: I remember it so well because it was a carefree childhood moment with a real sense of camaraderie. Nobody had phones, so the game was our whole world.

part3.q: Why do you think children today spend less time on outdoor games than in the past?
part3.a: There are a few reasons. Many families live in tall apartment blocks where there is no safe place to play, and parents worry about traffic. On top of that, smartphones and online games offer instant entertainment, so children rarely feel the need to go outside.

part3.q: Do you think team games teach children skills that individual activities cannot?
part3.a: Yes, because team games force children to cooperate and communicate. You learn to share responsibility, accept losing gracefully and resolve arguments quickly. A child who only plays alone on a tablet rarely gets the chance to practise these social skills.

part3.q: Should schools in cities with little open space still make time for physical play?
part3.a: Absolutely. Even if there is no field, schools can use rooftops, corridors or indoor halls for simple games and exercises. Physical activity helps students concentrate in class and burn off energy, so it supports academic results rather than competing with them.

part3.q: How have traditional games changed as technology has become more widespread?
part3.a: Many have moved onto screens. Ludo and carrom, for example, now exist as phone apps that children play against strangers. This is convenient, but I think something is lost, since the laughter and physical closeness of playing face to face disappears.

title: Describe a skill you taught yourself without attending any classes.
prompts: what the skill is
how you went about learning it
what difficulties you faced along the way
and explain how this skill has been useful to you.
angles: Learning to edit videos on my laptop
Learning to cook biryani by experiment

steps.label: Introduction
steps.anchor: The skill I taught myself is ...
sentences: The skill I taught myself is basic graphic design, using free software on my laptop. I never attended a single class for it.
It feels a bit unusual to say that, but I am quite proud of it.

steps.label: How I learned
sentences: I started when I was in my second year at university because our debating club needed posters. I watched tutorials on YouTube, copied simple layouts and then tried to create my own. It was mostly trial and error, with hours of experimenting each weekend.

steps.label: Difficulties
sentences: The learning curve was steep. At first my designs looked messy, the colours clashed and I kept losing files because I did not understand layers. I almost gave up after one poster took me an entire night, but a senior student gave me honest feedback that helped a lot.
Sometimes I felt it was hopeless, yet I kept going because I enjoyed the small improvements.

steps.label: Benefits
sentences: Now this skill has been really useful. I design flyers for friends' events, and I even earn a little pocket money from small business pages on Facebook.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: Looking back, I am proud that I learned it through hands-on experience. It made me realise that patience matters more than talent.

part3.q: Is it better to learn a new skill alone or with a teacher? Why?
part3.a: It depends on the skill. A teacher saves time and corrects mistakes before they become habits, which is vital for things like swimming or driving. But learning alone builds independence and lets you move at your own speed, so I would say beginners benefit from a mix of both.

part3.q: Why do some people give up learning something new so quickly?
part3.a: Often because they expect fast results. When progress is slow, they feel foolish and compare themselves with experts. Others lack a clear reason for learning, so when things get hard there is nothing to keep them going.

part3.q: Do you think schools should spend more time teaching practical skills rather than academic subjects?
part3.a: I believe there should be a better balance. Subjects like maths and science are essential, but students also need budgeting, first aid or basic coding. In Bangladesh, many graduates struggle to find jobs because they lack practical abilities, so some change is needed.

part3.q: How has the internet changed the way people acquire new abilities?
part3.a: It has made learning almost free and available at any hour. Anyone with a mobile connection can watch a tutorial, join a forum or take a short course. The downside is information overload, so learners need discipline to choose reliable sources and actually practise.

title: Describe a sports match that you watched and found exciting.
prompts: what the match was and who was playing
where you watched it and who you were with
what happened during the match
and explain why it was so exciting.

steps.label: Introduction
steps.anchor: The match I have in mind is ...
sentences: The match I have in mind is a cricket game between Bangladesh and India in the Asia Cup. It was one of those matches you simply cannot forget.
Every Bangladeshi supporter I know remembers that tournament.

steps.label: Setting
sentences: I watched it at my friend Rafi's house with about ten classmates, all crowded around a single television. We had brought snacks and wore our team jerseys, and the atmosphere was electric even before the first ball.

steps.label: The match
sentences: Bangladesh batted first and struggled early, losing three wickets cheaply. India then set a tough target, and for a while the room went completely silent.
My cousin kept pacing and could not even sit down to eat.

steps.label: The turning point
steps.anchor: Then, in the last few minutes, ...
sentences: Then, in the last over, we needed eight runs, and the final ball decided everything. Our batsman hit a boundary and the whole street erupted with cheering, horns and fireworks. People were hugging strangers on the road.

steps.label: Why it thrilled me
sentences: It was so exciting because it was a nail-biting finish where nothing was certain until the end. I was literally on the edge of my seat, and my voice was gone the next day.

part3.q: Why are some sports far more popular than others in Bangladesh?
part3.a: Cricket and football dominate because they are cheap to play and everyone understands the rules. You only need a bat, a ball and some open ground. Success on the international stage matters too, since people love supporting a winning national team.

part3.q: Do you think professional athletes are paid too much compared with other professionals?
part3.a: In some cases yes, especially in football, where players earn millions while nurses and teachers struggle. However, athletes have short careers and bring huge revenue through broadcasting and sponsorship. So I think the pay reflects the market, even if it feels unfair.

part3.q: Can watching sport together bring a community or a nation closer?
part3.a: I strongly think so. During big tournaments, people forget their differences and celebrate as one. When Bangladesh wins, strangers share sweets and flags on the street, which creates a powerful sense of national pride.

part3.q: Is it more enjoyable to watch a match in a stadium or at home? Why?
part3.a: The stadium offers an unmatched atmosphere, with chanting crowds and live drama. At home, though, you get replays, commentary and comfort, and it is much cheaper. Personally I prefer a stadium for big finals and my sofa for ordinary games.

title: Describe an activity that helps you unwind after a tiring or stressful week.
prompts: what the activity is
when and where you usually do it
whether you do it alone or with others
and explain how it helps you feel better.
angles: Cooking a favourite meal on Fridays

steps.label: Introduction
steps.anchor: The activity I turn to is ...
sentences: The activity that helps me wind down is walking by the lake at Dhanmondi after sunset. It sounds simple, but it works wonders for me.
It is nothing fancy, but it has become a weekly ritual that I really look forward to.

steps.label: When and where
sentences: I usually go on Thursday evenings, once my classes and assignments are over for the week. I wear comfortable shoes, put on a calm playlist and walk slowly for around forty minutes.

steps.label: Alone or together
sentences: Most of the time I go alone because I like to take my mind off things without making conversation. Occasionally my sister joins me, and we stop for a cup of tea and a fuchka from a vendor near the gate.

steps.label: How it helps
sentences: It helps because the fresh air and gentle exercise clear my head. By the time I get home, the tension in my shoulders has gone and I sleep much better. It is a real change of pace after a week of screens and deadlines.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: For me, it is the best way to recharge my batteries. I feel ready to face Saturday morning with a fresh mind.
I honestly think everyone needs one habit like this.

part3.q: Why do people in modern cities seem to feel more stressed than people in the past?
part3.a: Cities are noisy, crowded and fast. In Dhaka, people spend hours in traffic and work long hours under constant pressure. Smartphones also mean work follows them home, so they never fully switch off the way earlier generations could.

part3.q: Is it better to relax by doing something active or by doing nothing at all?
part3.a: I think both have value, but active relaxation usually works better for me. A walk or a game of football releases tension physically, while lying on a sofa often leaves me restless. Still, on very exhausting days, resting quietly is exactly what the body needs.

part3.q: Should employers give workers more free time for leisure activities?
part3.a: Yes, because rested employees are more productive and make fewer mistakes. Companies that offer flexible hours or proper weekends often see lower burnout. Employers should see leisure as an investment, not a waste.

part3.q: How important is it for young people to have hobbies alongside their studies?
part3.a: Very important. Hobbies protect students from burnout and teach them skills that exams never measure, like creativity or teamwork. In Bangladesh, competition is intense, so a hobby can be the one space where young people feel relaxed.

title: Talk about a time when you took part in a community or volunteer activity.
prompts: what the activity was and who organised it
what you did there
who else took part
and explain what you gained from the experience.
angles: Teaching children at a free evening school

steps.label: Introduction
sentences: I once took part in a food distribution drive during Ramadan, organised by a youth club in my area. I joined because a friend invited me, and I wanted to give something back.
It was my first experience of that kind, so I was a bit nervous.

steps.label: What we did
sentences: My role was to pack rice, lentils, oil and dates into bags and then deliver them to low-income families. We packed over two hundred bags on a Saturday morning, then walked through narrow lanes in a nearby slum, knocking on doors. It was tiring work, but very organised.

steps.label: The people involved
sentences: About twenty volunteers took part, mostly university students and a few older members of the club. A retired teacher led the group, and he made sure every family received the same amount and was treated politely.

steps.label: What I gained
sentences: What I gained was a real sense of purpose. I saw how small a bag of rice looks next to a family's needs, yet how grateful people were. It made my own problems feel smaller.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: Overall, I learned that community spirit starts with ordinary people willing to lend a hand. I have joined two more drives since then.
It showed me how much can be done together.

part3.q: Why do some people volunteer while others never do?
part3.a: I think it depends on upbringing and free time. People raised in families that value helping others often volunteer naturally. Others work long hours or simply have never been asked, so they assume it is not for them.

part3.q: Should schools require students to do voluntary work?
part3.a: I think it would be beneficial if it is well organised. Required volunteering exposes students to realities they might never see otherwise and builds empathy. However, it should be meaningful, not just a box to tick, or students will resent it.

part3.q: What kinds of volunteering do you think are most needed in Bangladesh today?
part3.a: Disaster relief is crucial, since floods and cyclones hit regularly. Education support is also needed, such as tutoring children in remote areas. Finally, environmental clean-ups would help our rivers and cities, which suffer from heavy pollution.

part3.q: Is giving time more valuable than giving money to a good cause?
part3.a: Both matter, but time often creates a personal connection that money cannot. When you spend an afternoon with children or patients, you understand their needs better. That said, money can fund materials and salaries, so the best approach combines the two.

title: Describe something you made by hand, such as a craft, a drawing or a piece of clothing.
prompts: what you made
how and why you made it
what materials or tools you used
and explain how you felt about the finished result.
angles: A birthday card painted by hand

steps.label: Introduction
steps.anchor: Something I made by hand was ...
sentences: Something I made by hand was a kantha-style cushion cover, stitched from old saris. It was a gift for my grandmother's birthday.
I had never made anything like it before, so I was a little nervous.

steps.label: How and why I made it
steps.anchor: I decided to make it because ...
sentences: I decided to make it because she loves traditional embroidery and always complained that nobody in the family kept the skill alive. I wanted to show her I had been paying attention.

steps.label: Materials and tools
sentences: For this I needed soft cotton cloth from two worn saris, coloured thread, a needle and a small wooden frame. My aunt lent me the tools and taught me the basic running stitch.

steps.label: The process
sentences: It took me nearly three weeks of evenings. My first rows were uneven and I had to unpick them twice, but I slowly developed an eye for detail. I stitched a lotus pattern in the centre, because she once told me it was her favourite flower.

steps.label: My feelings
sentences: When I finished, I felt deeply satisfied, almost emotional. It was a labour of love, and when my grandmother held it and smiled, every crooked stitch felt worth it.
Now she keeps it on her bed and shows it to every guest.

part3.q: Why do people still value handmade items when machines can produce them cheaper?
part3.a: Because a handmade item carries personal effort and uniqueness. A machine can copy a thousand identical pieces, but nobody else will own exactly what an artisan made. People also feel emotionally connected to the story behind the object.

part3.q: Do you think traditional crafts in Bangladesh are in danger of disappearing?
part3.a: To some extent, yes. Younger people prefer stable office jobs, and cheap factory goods undercut craftsmen's prices. Crafts like jamdani weaving or nakshi kantha need years of training, so unless they are supported and promoted, the skills could fade.

part3.q: Should creative subjects get as much attention in school as maths and science?
part3.a: I believe so. Creative subjects develop imagination, problem solving and emotional expression, which are important in any career. In many Bangladeshi schools, art classes are treated as optional, and that sends the wrong message.

part3.q: Can a creative hobby become a successful career? Under what circumstances?
part3.a: Yes, if the person combines talent with business sense. Social media now lets crafters reach customers directly, as many home-based sellers on Facebook show. However, it requires consistency, quality and patience before income becomes stable.

title: Talk about a hobby that you would like to take up in the future.
prompts: what the hobby is
why it interests you
what you would need to get started

steps.label: Introduction
steps.anchor: A hobby I would love to take up is ...

It may sound ordinary, but it means a lot to me.

steps.label: Why it interests me
sentences: What attracts me is the idea of freezing small moments, like a rickshaw puller resting in the rain or light on the river at dawn. I follow a few photographers online, and their work makes me see ordinary places differently.

steps.label: What I would need
steps.anchor: To get started, I would need ...
sentences: To get started, I would need a decent camera, maybe a second-hand one to save money, and a basic course or at least some tutorials. I would also need time to walk around with it, ideally on weekends.
A cheap tripod would also be useful for night shots.

steps.label: Why I have not tried it
steps.anchor: The reason I have not begun is ...
sentences: The reason I have not begun is mainly money and my busy schedule. A good camera costs more than I can spare while I am preparing for IELTS, and I keep telling myself I will do it later.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: One day soon, I plan to buy a used camera after I get my result. I am keen on it, and I think it would be a hobby I could enjoy for life.

part3.q: Do people tend to change their hobbies as they get older? Why?
part3.a: Generally yes. Priorities, energy and income all change with age. A teenager might love football, but a middle-aged person may prefer gardening or reading. Responsibilities also reduce free time, so people choose calmer, more convenient pastimes.

part3.q: What stops adults from pursuing hobbies as much as children do?
part3.a: Mostly time and responsibility. Adults juggle work, family duties and long commutes, so leisure feels like a luxury. Many also feel guilty spending time on something that is not productive, which children never worry about.

part3.q: Are expensive hobbies more rewarding than cheap ones?
part3.a: Not necessarily. Reward depends on how much enjoyment and growth you get, not on cost. Some of the happiest people I know enjoy free hobbies like walking or sketching, while some expensive ones just become status symbols.

part3.q: How can having a shared hobby affect friendships?
part3.a: It usually strengthens them. You spend regular time together and share goals and jokes, which builds trust. For example, my cousins and I became much closer after we joined a cycling group, because we had something to look forward to each week.

title: Describe a day you spent outdoors with your family or friends, such as a picnic or a trip to a river or park.
prompts: where you went and when
who was with you
what you did during the day
and explain why you enjoyed it.
angles: A family day at a village pond

steps.label: Introduction
steps.anchor: The day I want to describe is ...
sentences: The day I want to describe is a family picnic at Madhabkunda Waterfall in Moulvibazar, which we did last winter. It was a refreshing escape from city life.
It was one of the most relaxed days I have had.

steps.label: Where and who
sentences: We went early on a Friday morning with my parents, my two cousins and my uncle's family, around nine of us in a rented microbus. The drive took about four hours, and we sang old songs most of the way.

steps.label: What we did
sentences: Once we arrived, we walked down the forest path to the waterfall, took photos and splashed in the shallow pools. Then we spread a mat under the trees and ate parathas, boiled eggs and fruit that my mother had packed.

steps.label: A special moment
sentences: What I remember best is when my little cousin slipped into the water fully clothed and everyone burst out laughing. Even my serious uncle joined the splashing.

steps.label: Why I enjoyed it
sentences: I enjoyed it because it was real quality time without phones, and the open air felt like a breath of fresh air after months of studying. We returned tired but very happy.
I still look at the photos whenever I feel stressed.

part3.q: Why do many people in big cities rarely spend time in nature?
part3.a: Mainly because green space is scarce and travel is difficult. In Dhaka, getting out of the city can take hours because of traffic. People are also busy, so on weekends they usually choose to rest at home or visit malls.

part3.q: Do you think family outings are as important now as they were in the past?
part3.a: I think they are even more important now. Families spend less time together because everyone is on a screen or at work. An outing forces people to talk to each other and creates shared memories, which strengthen family bonds.

part3.q: What could local authorities do to make public outdoor spaces more attractive?
part3.a: They should keep existing parks clean, safe and well lit, and add benches, toilets and play areas. Planting more trees and restoring riverbanks would also help. Regular events like markets or cultural programmes could bring people in too.

part3.q: Is spending time outdoors good for children's development? In what ways?
part3.a: Yes, in many ways. Outdoor play improves physical health, balance and coordination, and exposure to nature can reduce anxiety. Children also learn creativity and teamwork when they invent games in open spaces, rather than following instructions on a screen.

phrases.m: time fully focused on loved ones

title: Describe a mobile app that you use almost every day.

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The app I use almost every day is ...

steps.label: How I found it
steps.anchor: I first came across it when ...
sentences: I first heard about it from my elder brother, who was working in Dhaka at the time. He sent me my pocket money through it, and I installed it that same evening because I was tired of waiting in queues.

steps.label: How I use it
sentences: These days I open it at least three or four times a day. I pay for my internet bill, split restaurant costs with friends and send money to my mother in the village. The interface is user-friendly, so even my grandmother learned to check her balance.

steps.label: Why it matters
steps.anchor: The main reason it matters to me is ...
sentences: It matters because it saves me a huge amount of time and stress. Before this, a simple payment could eat up half my afternoon in traffic. Now it takes thirty seconds, and I get an instant confirmation message.

steps.label: Wrap-up
steps.anchor: All in all, I would say ...
sentences: Honestly, it has become a handy tool that I could not imagine living without. If it stopped working for a day, my whole routine would be thrown off.

part3.q: Do you think people rely too much on apps to manage their daily lives?
part3.a: I think many people do lean on apps too heavily. They use them for reminders, navigation, payments and even decisions about what to eat. Apps are convenient, but I have seen friends who cannot find a familiar road without a map, so some basic skills are being lost.

part3.q: How have mobile apps changed the way businesses in Bangladesh work?
part3.a: They have changed things enormously. Small online shops on Facebook now take orders and payments through apps, and delivery riders are tracked live. A friend of mine sells handmade bags from home and reaches customers in Chattogram that she never could have met before.

part3.q: Should there be limits on how much personal data apps can collect?
part3.a: Yes, I believe there should be clear limits. Apps often collect location, contacts and browsing habits that they do not really need. If that data leaks, ordinary people could suffer fraud, so companies ought to ask permission and explain simply what they store.

part3.q: Will apps eventually replace the need for traditional services such as banks and shops?
part3.a: I think they will replace some services but not all of them. Banking is already moving to phones, and many people shop online. However, older people and those in remote villages still prefer face to face help, so physical shops and branches will probably stay for a long time.

title: Describe a television programme or web series that your family enjoyed watching together.
prompts: what the programme was about
when and where your family watched it
who liked it most
and explain why it appealed to your family.
angles: a drama serial on BTV or a channel
a web series on a streaming app

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The programme I have in mind is ...
sentences: The programme I have in mind is a family drama serial we watched during the last Ramadan. It was the kind of show that everybody in the house agreed on, which is quite rare.

steps.label: What it was about
sentences: The story followed a joint family in an old Dhaka house and the funny, sometimes emotional problems between three generations. It had a gripping storyline, with a small twist at the end of nearly every episode.

steps.label: When and who liked it
sentences: We watched it after iftar in the living room, all sitting on one sofa and a couple of mats. My mother liked it most, I think, because she kept predicting what would happen next and was often proud when she was right. My father pretended not to care but never missed one episode.

steps.label: Why it appealed
steps.anchor: I think it appealed to us because ...
sentences: It appealed to us because the characters felt real, like our own relatives. Everyone could laugh at the same jokes, and it gave us a talking point at dinner. That is unusual in a time when we all stare at our own phones.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: Looking back, those evenings were less about the show and more about being together.

part3.q: Do you think television still plays an important role in people's lives now that streaming is popular?
part3.a: I think it still matters, especially for older people and in smaller towns where streaming is too costly or the connection is poor. Television also brings the whole family together at a fixed time. For big events like cricket matches or national news, it is still the first thing many people switch on.

part3.q: Is it a good thing that families often watch different content on separate devices?
part3.a: I would say it is a mixed thing. On one hand, everyone enjoys what they personally like. On the other hand, families lose shared time because each person is lost in their own screen. A good compromise is to keep at least one evening for watching something together.

part3.q: Should the government control what is shown on television?
part3.a: I think some control is reasonable, for example protecting children from violent or very inappropriate content. But too much control can become censorship and stop honest journalism. A better approach is clear age ratings and rules, with the final choice left to parents.

part3.q: How much influence do TV dramas have on the way young people behave?
part3.a: The influence is quite strong, to be honest. Young people copy hairstyles, slang and even attitudes from popular dramas. Some of it is harmless, but when shows glamorise rudeness or unrealistic lifestyles, teenagers may feel their own lives are not good enough.

phrases.m: a plot that holds your attention
watch many episodes in a row

title: Describe a time when your internet connection or electricity failed at an important moment.
prompts: when and where it happened
what you were trying to do
how you dealt with the problem
and explain how the situation made you feel.

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The incident I remember happened when ...
sentences: The incident I remember happened last year during my university admission interview, which was held online. It was a Sunday afternoon at my home in Mirpur.

steps.label: Background
steps.anchor: At that moment I was trying to ...
sentences: I was trying to impress a panel of three teachers on a video call. Ten minutes in, the power went out in our whole area, and the Wi-Fi router died with it. The screen froze right in the middle of my answer.

steps.label: What I did
steps.anchor: The first thing I did was ...
sentences: I did not panic at first. I grabbed my phone, switched to mobile data and rejoined, though the connection was patchy. When it kept dropping, I sent them a short message and called the department number, explaining that it was a technical glitch. Luckily the panel agreed to a short break.

steps.label: Feelings
sentences: I felt a mix of fear and embarrassment, because it came out of the blue and I had prepared for weeks. My heart was pounding and my hands were shaking. Once they were understanding, I calmed down.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: Since then, I always keep a power bank and a backup plan ready. I also tell people early if something might go wrong.

part3.q: Are people too dependent on the internet in their work and studies?
part3.a: Yes, I think we depend on it far too much. Students submit assignments, attend classes and even take exams online, so one hour without a connection can stop everything. We should still keep the habit of having offline notes and printed copies for important work.

part3.q: What problems do areas with poor connectivity face compared with well-connected cities?
part3.a: Rural and remote areas face slow speeds, frequent outages and high prices. Students there may miss online classes, and small farmers cannot check market prices easily. This widens the gap between them and people in Dhaka, who enjoy fast broadband and many more opportunities.

part3.q: Whose responsibility is it to improve internet access, the government or private companies?
part3.a: I think it should be shared. The government must build the basic infrastructure, such as fibre cables to villages, because private companies find it unprofitable. Companies, in turn, should offer fair prices and keep their service reliable. Without cooperation, ordinary users keep paying for poor quality.

part3.q: Do you think life would be better or worse if we spent less time online?
part3.a: I think a little less would be better. We would probably sleep earlier, talk more face to face and read more books. But the internet also gives education and jobs, so the real answer is balance, using it with purpose instead of scrolling for hours.

an alternative if the first fails
signal that keeps cutting in and out

title: Talk about a piece of news that you read or heard recently and found interesting.

where and how you came across it
what you thought when you first heard it

steps.label: Opening

sentences: The piece of news I want to talk about is a report I read last week about a group of students from Rajshahi who built a low-cost water filter for flood-hit villages. It was a short but inspiring story.

steps.label: Where I found it
sentences: I came across it while scrolling through a news website during my lunch break, and then my uncle mentioned it on a phone call. Since two reliable outlets had covered it, I was fairly sure it was not fake news.

steps.label: My first reaction
steps.anchor: When I first read it, I thought ...
sentences: When I first read the headline, I was a bit doubtful, because many stories online sound too good to be true. But as I read further, I saw photos, quotes from villagers and the cost details. I thought, this is real, and it is practical.

steps.label: Why it caught me
steps.anchor: What really caught my attention was ...
sentences: What really caught my attention was how simple the idea was. They used local materials and charcoal, and the whole filter cost less than five hundred taka. It showed me that young people can solve serious problems without expensive equipment.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: It reminded me to keep up with current events, because good news like this is easy to miss.

part3.q: Where do most people in Bangladesh get their news from today?
part3.a: Most people, especially the young, get news from Facebook and YouTube now. Older people still depend on television, and some read newspapers in the morning. Smartphones are cheap, so the news is simply the thing that arrives on the screen without anyone searching for it.

part3.q: Why is it sometimes difficult to tell whether a news story is true?
part3.a: It is difficult because anyone can post anything, and false stories are often written to look professional. Photos can be edited, and emotional headlines spread faster than corrections. I always check whether a reliable outlet is also reporting the story before I believe or share it.

part3.q: Do you think journalists should be allowed to report anything they find?
part3.a: I think they should report the truth, but with limits. Journalists have a duty to expose corruption, so they need freedom. However, publishing private details of victims or unverified rumours can ruin lives. Responsible reporting means considering the harm as well as the public interest.

part3.q: Is it better to follow the news every day or only occasionally?
part3.a: I think following it occasionally is healthier for most people. Constant news, especially bad news, makes you anxious and wastes time. Checking once a day from a trustworthy source keeps you informed without stress. Of course, people in certain jobs, such as politics, need to follow it closely.

title: Describe an electronic gadget that you would like to own.
prompts: what the gadget is
what it can do
how you found out about it
and explain why you want it.

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The gadget I would love to own is ...
sentences: The gadget I would love to own is a good e-reader, something like a Kindle. I have wanted one for almost two years now.

steps.label: What it can do
steps.anchor: What makes it special is that ...
sentences: It is a thin, lightweight device with a screen that looks like real paper. It can store thousands of books, lets me change the font size and works for weeks on a single charge. The display does not strain my eyes even in bright sunlight.

steps.label: How I found out
steps.anchor: I first heard about it when ...
sentences: I first found out about it from a senior at university who always carried hers. She let me try it, and I was amazed. Later I watched several review videos, and I compared prices, though imported ones are quite expensive in Bangladesh.

steps.label: Why I want it
steps.anchor: The main reason I want it is ...
sentences: I want it because I love reading, but heavy books are hard to carry on the crowded bus to campus. Also, many English novels and reference books are difficult to find in local bookshops. For me it would be worth the investment, since I would read far more.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: So, when I get my first salary, it is the first thing I will buy.

part3.q: Why do many people feel they have to buy the newest gadgets?
part3.a: I think it is mostly social pressure and advertising. Companies make a new model look like a status symbol, and friends compare phones. Many people also fear missing out on features. In reality, the older device often works fine, but nobody wants to look behind the trend.

part3.q: Do you think modern devices are designed to break after a short time?
part3.a: There is some truth in that. Many phones get slower after a couple of years, batteries are sealed in and repairs are costly. Companies earn more when we replace things often. I think this is partly deliberate, and that is why consumers should demand longer warranties and repairable designs.

part3.q: How have gadgets changed the way young people spend their free time?
part3.a: Gadgets have changed leisure a lot. Young people used to play cricket in the street or visit friends, but now many stay indoors with games or videos. On the positive side, they also learn skills like editing and coding. The key is not letting devices replace outdoor activity completely.

part3.q: What are the effects of electronic waste, and who should deal with it?
part3.a: E-waste is a growing problem because old phones and batteries contain toxic metals that pollute soil and water. I think producers should take responsibility by offering take-back and recycling schemes. The government should enforce rules, and individuals can help by repairing or donating devices.

phrases.m: good value for the money spent
spend a lot of money on

title: Describe an online video or channel from which you learned something useful.
prompts: what the video or channel is
how you came across it
what you learned from it
and explain why you would recommend it to others.
angles: a coding or maths tutorial channel

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The channel I want to talk about is ...
sentences: The channel I want to talk about is a YouTube channel that teaches spreadsheet skills, mainly Excel. The presenter explains everything calmly, in plain English, with examples from real offices.

steps.label: How I found it
sentences: I stumbled on it two years ago when I had to prepare a data report for a university project and had no idea how to begin. I typed my problem into the search bar, and one of his videos was the top result. After that I subscribed straight away.

steps.label: What I learned
steps.anchor: One thing I picked up is ...
sentences: The most valuable thing I picked up was how to use formulas and pivot tables to organise large sets of data. Each video is a step-by-step tutorial with a downloadable file, so I could practise along. Within a month, a task that used to take me three hours took twenty minutes.

steps.label: Why I recommend it
sentences: I would recommend it to others because the lessons are short, free and well structured. You do not need any background, and you can pause or replay any part. Many of my classmates now use it, and some even mention it in job interviews.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: To sum up, it is an excellent example of educational content done well.

part3.q: Can online videos replace classroom teaching? Why or why not?
part3.a: I do not think they can replace classroom teaching completely. Videos are great for explaining a concept, but a teacher can answer questions, notice confusion and motivate students. I believe the best approach combines both, with videos for revision and the classroom for discussion.

part3.q: Why do some people trust information from social media influencers so easily?
part3.a: Many people trust influencers because they look friendly and seem like ordinary people. They share their personal stories, so followers feel a close bond. However, an influencer may be paid to promote a product, and young viewers rarely check that. Popularity is often confused with expertise.

part3.q: What are the dangers of learning everything from the internet?
part3.a: The biggest danger is misinformation, since anyone can upload a video, whether or not they know the subject. Learners may also get only scattered knowledge with no proper foundation. In addition, it is easy to get distracted by unrelated videos and waste an entire evening.

part3.q: How might education change in the next twenty years because of technology?
part3.a: I expect classes to become more flexible and personalised. Students may use AI tutors that adapt to their level, and virtual labs could let rural students do experiments that their schools cannot afford. Teachers will still be needed, but more as guides than as sources of facts.

phrases.m: lesson that follows each stage in order
learn it casually, without formal study
as fast or slow as I like

title: Describe a time when you helped an older person learn to use a piece of technology.
prompts: who the person was and what they wanted to learn
what device or technology it was
how you explained it to them
and explain how you felt about the experience.
angles: an elderly neighbour with video calls

steps.label: Opening
sentences: The person I helped was my grandmother, who lives with us in Sylhet. She is seventy-three and had never used anything more complicated than a basic keypad phone.

steps.label: Who and what
steps.anchor: What she wanted to learn was ...
sentences: She wanted to learn how to make video calls, because my uncle works in Dubai and she misses him badly. So I set her up with a smartphone and WhatsApp, which was a big step for her.

steps.label: How I explained
steps.anchor: I tried to walk her through it by ...
sentences: I did not just give instructions, I walked her through it slowly. First, I made the icons bigger and wrote the steps in Bangla on a small card. Then we practised calling my uncle together again and again until she could get the hang of it. She was nervous about pressing the wrong button, so I told her nothing would break.

steps.label: Feelings
sentences: I felt very proud and a bit emotional. The first time she saw my uncle's face on screen and started crying and laughing together, I almost cried too. It also taught me to be patient, since I had to repeat things many times.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: Now she calls him every Friday on her own, and that makes my effort feel worthwhile.

part3.q: Why do many older people find new technology difficult to use?
part3.a: I think it is because they did not grow up with these devices, so the logic is unfamiliar. Menus, icons and passwords are confusing, and they fear making a mistake. Also, apps update often and the layout changes, so just when they learn one thing, it is different again.

part3.q: Is there a risk that older people will be left behind in a digital society?
part3.a: Yes, there is a real risk. Services like banking, ticketing and government forms are moving online, so those without digital skills may struggle to get help. Some older people are also easy targets for scams. We need to make sure basic services stay available offline too.

part3.q: Whose job should it be to teach people how to use technology, family or public services?
part3.a: I think it should be shared. Family members can offer patient, personal help at home, which is the most effective. But not everyone has relatives nearby, so public services like community centres, libraries or union offices should hold simple training sessions for seniors, ideally in Bangla.

part3.q: Do you think technology brings generations closer together or pushes them apart?
part3.a: I believe it can do both, depending on how it is used. Video calls keep grandparents connected to grandchildren abroad, which is wonderful. Yet when everyone in a room is on their own phone, the generations talk less. It brings us closer only if we use it to share time, not to avoid it.

phrases.m: gap between those with and without tech access

title: Talk about a photograph you took on your phone or camera that you particularly like.
prompts: what the photograph shows
when and where you took it
what the situation was at the time
and explain why it means a lot to you.
angles: a street scene in old Dhaka

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The photograph I want to describe shows ...
sentences: The photograph I want to describe is one I took of my father and my little sister on a boat at Sundarbans. It is a candid shot of them laughing at something outside the frame.

steps.label: What it shows
sentences: It shows the two of them in the front of the boat, with green mangrove trees behind and soft golden light on the water. My sister is pointing at a bird, and my father is leaning down to look.

steps.label: When and where
steps.anchor: The situation at that moment was ...
sentences: I took it on my phone two winters ago, during our first proper family holiday in years. The situation was quite chaotic, because the boat was rocking and I nearly dropped my phone. But I pressed the button at the right second and captured the moment.

steps.label: Why it matters
steps.anchor: It means a lot to me because ...
sentences: It means a lot to me because my father is usually very busy and serious, and this is one of the rare photos where he looks completely relaxed. Since then he has become busier, so the picture is a fond memory of a time when we were all together.

steps.label: Wrap-up
steps.anchor: So whenever I look at it, ...
sentences: So whenever I look at it, I feel calm, and it motivates me to plan another trip.

part3.q: Why do people take so many more photos now than they did in the past?
part3.a: Mainly because cameras are now in every phone, and taking a picture costs nothing. In the past, film was expensive, so people saved it for special occasions. Social media has also made sharing part of daily life, so many people photograph their meals and outfits just to post them.

part3.q: Do you think sharing photos online has any negative effects on privacy?
part3.a: Yes, I think it does. People often upload pictures with their location, school uniform or home visible, and strangers can use that information. Also, photos of children or friends are posted without permission. We should think twice and use privacy settings before sharing anything personal.

part3.q: Is a photograph a better way to remember an event than a written account?
part3.a: I think they work best together. A photo shows how a place or a person looked, which words cannot capture exactly. But a written account adds feelings, context and details that the camera misses, like why something was funny. For me, a short caption under a photo is the ideal.

part3.q: Will professional photography still be needed when everyone has a good camera in their pocket?
part3.a: I think professionals will still be needed. A phone can take a nice picture, but weddings, product shoots and news events need skill in lighting, composition and editing. Also, clients want reliability and quality, which a casual snap cannot always provide. The job will change, but it will not disappear.

phrases.m: light from the sun, not a flash
how things are arranged in a photo

title: Describe a skill you learned that has been useful in your studies or work.
prompts: what the skill is
how and where you learned it
how often you use it now
and explain why it has been so useful to you.

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The skill I want to talk about is ...
sentences: The skill I want to talk about is time management, specifically planning my week on paper. It sounds simple, but it has changed how I study.

steps.label: How I learned it
sentences: I learned it in my first year at university, when I failed to submit two assignments on time. A senior student showed me how to divide big tasks into small daily goals. After a month of hands-on practice, with plenty of mistakes, it became a habit.

steps.label: How often I use it
sentences: Now I use it every single day. On Sunday evening I write down my classes, deadlines and revision hours, and every night I tick off what I finished. I also add some free time, since planning only work is a mistake.

steps.label: Why it is useful
sentences: It has been useful because I feel much less stressed before exams, and my grades have improved. It is also a transferable skill, so I can use it in an office job later. During my internship last summer, my supervisor praised me for always finishing work before the deadline.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: In short, it is a small skill that has given me a great deal of control over my life.

part3.q: Which skills do you think young people most need to find a good job today?
part3.a: I think communication, digital skills and problem solving are the most needed. Almost every job now requires basic computer knowledge, and employers want people who can explain ideas clearly and work with others. Learning English helps a lot in Bangladesh, especially for jobs in international companies.

part3.q: Is it better to learn practical skills at school or on the job?
part3.a: I believe both are important. School gives the foundation and theory, but practical skills are often learned better on the job, where you face real situations. The ideal is for schools to include internships or workshops, so students are not completely new when they start working.

part3.q: How have online courses changed the way people learn new skills?
part3.a: Online courses have made learning much more accessible. Someone in a small town can now study from a good teacher abroad for a low price, at their own pace. The weakness is that many people start and never finish, because there is nobody pushing them. Self-discipline is essential.

part3.q: Do you think employers value skills more than university degrees?
part3.a: It depends on the field. In engineering or medicine, a degree is essential. However, in areas such as design, marketing or programming, many employers care more about what you can actually do, so a good portfolio can matter more. I think skills are gradually becoming more important.

phrases.m: hard to learn at the start

title: Describe a time when you worked with others to finish a task.
prompts: what the task was
who you worked with
what your role in the team was
and explain how you felt about the result.

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The time I want to describe is when ...
sentences: The time I want to describe is when my classmates and I organised a charity book fair at our university last winter. We wanted to collect books for a village library near Gazipur.

steps.label: The task and team
steps.anchor: There were five of us, and ...
sentences: There were six of us, and we had only three weeks to get it done. We had to ask for donations, book a hall, make posters and manage the stall on the day. At first we argued about who should do what, but we soon decided to pull together.

steps.label: My role
steps.anchor: My role in the team was ...
sentences: My role in the team was handling publicity and the budget. I designed posters, wrote Facebook posts and kept a record of every taka spent. Others looked after the venue and the volunteers, so there was a clear division of labour, and everyone pulled their weight.

steps.label: Feelings about the result
steps.anchor: When it was finished, I felt ...
sentences: When it was finished, I felt proud and relieved. We collected more than eight hundred books and nearly twenty thousand taka for the library. Seeing strangers donate so generously, I realised our tiring weeks of work had been worth it.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: That experience showed me that a group can achieve far more than one person alone.

part3.q: Why do some people prefer working alone rather than in a team?
part3.a: Some people feel they can work faster and keep control of quality when they are alone. Others have had bad experiences with team members who did not contribute, so they stop trusting groups. Introverts also tend to think better in silence. Personally, I think both styles are fine if the work gets done.

part3.q: What qualities make someone a good team member?
part3.a: I think reliability is the most important quality, because the whole team suffers when someone misses a deadline. Good listening and respect for other opinions matter too. Finally, a positive attitude is contagious. In my own group, the person who stayed cheerful during stressful moments kept us all going.

part3.q: Should schools give more group projects to students?
part3.a: Yes, I think so, as long as they are well organised. Group projects teach communication, leadership and compromise, which exams cannot measure. However, teachers must make sure marks are fair, so that hard-working students are not carrying lazy ones. Short tasks with clear roles work best.

part3.q: How can a manager deal with conflict between team members?
part3.a: A good manager should first listen to both sides privately, without taking sides, to understand the real cause. Then they can bring everyone together to discuss a practical solution and agree on clear responsibilities. Ignoring a conflict usually makes it worse, so acting early is better.

phrases.m: do your fair share of work
use what each person does best

title: Describe a piece of advice about study or work that you have never forgotten.
prompts: who gave you the advice
what the advice was
when you received it
and explain how it has influenced you.

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The piece of advice that has stayed with me is ...
sentences: The piece of advice I will never forget came from my maths teacher in Class Ten. It was a simple sentence, but it changed how I study.

steps.label: Who and when
sentences: I was sitting in his office after a mock exam in Dhaka, feeling crushed because I had failed badly. He was a quiet man, and I had never expected him to speak to me so directly. That was about six years ago.

steps.label: The advice
sentences: He said, 'Do not measure yourself by one result; measure yourself by what you do every single day.' He told me to study just two focused hours daily instead of cramming all night before the exam. I took his words on board, though I doubted them at first.

steps.label: How it influenced me
sentences: Since then I have kept a small daily routine, and my scores climbed steadily. It also taught me to stay calm when things go wrong, which helped me during my university admission test. I now see that consistency matters more than talent.
It sounded simple, but I could feel it was true.
I try to pass on the same attitude to others.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: That is why I still repeat his sentence to younger cousins. It was a real turning point for me.

part3.q: Who usually gives the best career advice to young people, parents or teachers?
part3.a: I think teachers often give the more practical guidance, because they see students' strengths over several years. Parents, on the other hand, tend to worry about security, so their advice is sometimes too cautious. For example, my teacher noticed my interest in data long before my family did.

part3.q: Do people today listen to advice less than in the past?
part3.a: I would say people listen less, mainly because answers are only a click away. Young people check videos and forums rather than asking an elder. However, when the decision is serious, such as choosing a degree, most of them still seek a trusted voice.

part3.q: Is it wise to follow the advice of older generations about careers?
part3.a: It is wise to listen, but not to follow blindly. Older generations have real experience, yet the job market has changed enormously, and some of their favourite careers are now crowded. A sensible approach is to weigh their wisdom against current job prospects, as my uncle did when he urged me to look at IT.

part3.q: How important is it to have a mentor at work?
part3.a: I believe a mentor is extremely valuable, especially in the first few years of work. A good mentor shortens your learning curve and helps you avoid costly mistakes. In many Bangladeshi offices, juniors who have a senior to guide them get promoted noticeably faster.

phrases.m: a wise saying someone gives you
study hard at the last minute
time needed to learn a skill

title: Describe a deadline that you found difficult to meet.
prompts: what the work was and who set the deadline
why it was difficult to finish on time
what you did to manage the situation
and explain what you learned from the experience.
angles: a work report for my manager

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: I would like to talk about ...
sentences: I'd like to talk about a final-year research report that was extremely hard to finish on time. My supervisor set the deadline, and it was just ten days away when I truly started.

steps.label: The work
sentences: The report needed a survey of two hundred students, data analysis, and around five thousand words of writing. I had been procrastinating for weeks, telling myself there was plenty of time. Then my supervisor reminded me that no extensions would be given.

steps.label: Why it was difficult
sentences: The main problem was that load-shedding hit our area for hours every evening, so my laptop kept dying. Several survey participants also failed to reply, which delayed the analysis. I felt completely at the mercy of events outside my control.

steps.label: What I did
sentences: I made a day-by-day plan and moved to a university library that had a generator. I burned the midnight oil for four nights and asked a friend to proofread the draft. I submitted it two hours before the cut-off.
Honestly, I almost panicked, and I did not sleep well that week.
The experience really changed my work habits for good.

steps.label: What I learned
steps.anchor: The lesson I took away is ...
sentences: I learned never to leave big tasks until the end. Now I break any project into small daily targets.

part3.q: Why do some people leave work until the last minute?
part3.a: Mostly because the task feels huge and unpleasant, so they delay the first step. Others believe they work better with a looming deadline, though this is often just an excuse. I used to be exactly like that until a late submission cost me marks.

part3.q: Does working under pressure bring out the best in people?
part3.a: To some extent, yes. A little pressure sharpens focus and can push people to finish quickly. But heavy, constant pressure leads to stress and careless mistakes, so the best results usually come from steady, planned effort rather than a last-minute rush.

part3.q: How can schools help students manage their time better?
part3.a: Schools could teach planning as a real subject, using timetables and weekly goals. Teachers might also set smaller milestones for big assignments instead of a single final date. In Bangladesh, where students face heavy exam loads, this would reduce panic considerably.

part3.q: Are strict deadlines good or bad for creativity?
part3.a: I think rigid deadlines can limit creativity, particularly in design or writing, where ideas need time to develop. On the other hand, having no deadline at all often means nothing gets done. A flexible deadline with clear checkpoints seems the best balance.

phrases.m: finish on or before the due date
finishing at the very last moment

title: Describe a job that you think is very important for your community.
prompts: what the job is
what the people who do it have to do every day
what training or qualities it requires
and explain why you think it is important for society.
angles: a nurse in a government hospital
a garbage collector in the city

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: One job I consider vital is ...
sentences: A job I consider extremely important for my community is that of a village doctor, or a community health worker. I have seen how much our area depends on them.

steps.label: Daily work
sentences: In my grandparents' village, the health worker starts early, visiting patients at home when they cannot travel. She checks blood pressure, gives vaccines to children, and advises pregnant women. She also handles emergencies, often at night and in heavy monsoon rain.

steps.label: Training and qualities
steps.anchor: To do this well, you need ...
sentences: She completed a one-year medical training course, but the real skills come from experience. Above all, she needs patience, because many patients are frightened and some distrust medicine. Honesty and stamina are equally essential.
It is exhausting work, and she rarely complains about it, which impressed me deeply.

steps.label: Why it matters
steps.anchor: The reason I admire this job is ...
sentences: The nearest hospital is almost two hours away, so without her, minor illnesses would become serious. When my grandfather had a high fever last year, she recognised the danger and arranged transport quickly. That decision probably saved his life.
Because of her, many families in the village trust modern medicine now.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: All in all, these workers are the backbone of rural health, and they deserve far more recognition.

part3.q: Why are some important jobs paid less than others?
part3.a: Often pay reflects market demand rather than social value. Jobs like banking bring profit to companies, so they pay more, while teaching and nursing are mostly funded by tight public budgets. It is unfair, because those workers shape people's lives directly.

part3.q: Should the government raise salaries for jobs like teaching and nursing?
part3.a: Yes, I strongly believe so. Higher salaries would attract talented graduates who currently choose private companies. In Bangladesh, many good teachers leave for tuition centres because school pay is low. Better wages would improve the quality of education for everyone.

part3.q: How might technology change the jobs people do in the future?
part3.a: Technology will probably automate repetitive tasks such as data entry and basic customer service. But jobs that need empathy, like nursing and teaching, will remain human. New roles in areas such as app development and data analysis will also keep growing.

part3.q: Do young people today respect all kinds of work equally?
part3.a: Not always, I'm afraid. Many young people prefer office jobs and look down on manual work like farming or cleaning. This attitude is slowly changing, but we still need to teach that every honest job contributes to society.

title: Describe a time when you helped a classmate or colleague with their work.

what problem they had
how you helped them

steps.label: Opening
sentences: I remember helping a classmate named Rafi with a statistics assignment in my second year at university. He was a nice guy but was falling behind in that course.

steps.label: The problem
sentences: Rafi came from a Bangla-medium school, so the English textbook and technical terms confused him. The assignment was due in three days, and he was close to giving up. He admitted to me quietly that he felt embarrassed to ask the teacher.

steps.label: How I helped
sentences: I offered to meet him in the library for two evenings. First, I explained the key terms in simple Bangla, then we worked through sample problems step by step. I also shared my own notes and a few useful video links.

steps.label: How we felt
sentences: When he passed the assignment with a good mark, he was thrilled and bought me tea and singara. Honestly, I felt proud too, because teaching him made me understand the topic better. It strengthened our friendship as well.
He listened carefully and asked a lot of questions, which made teaching easy and pleasant.
We still study together before every exam.

steps.label: Wrap-up
steps.anchor: I think that experience showed me ...
sentences: It showed me that helping others also helps yourself.

part3.q: Is competition or cooperation more common among students in your country?
part3.a: I think both exist, but competition is stronger because of entrance exams and limited university seats. Students often keep good notes to themselves to stay ahead. However, close friends in study groups do cooperate, and that is where I learned the most.

part3.q: Why are some people unwilling to share knowledge with others?
part3.a: Some people fear that sharing knowledge will make them less valuable or help a rival. Others are simply too busy or insecure. In my experience, though, the people who share freely tend to gain respect and are the ones everyone wants on their team.

part3.q: How can workplaces encourage employees to support each other?
part3.a: Companies could reward teamwork rather than only individual targets, for instance through team bonuses. Regular workshops where staff teach each other new skills also help. Leaders should set an example by openly asking for and offering help.

part3.q: Does helping others at work always lead to rewards?
part3.a: Not necessarily in a direct way. Sometimes your effort goes unnoticed, and there is no promotion. But over time it builds trust and a good reputation, and people remember who helped them when they were struggling.

phrases.m: help from people of similar level

title: Describe an app or tool that helps you organise your study or work.
prompts: what the app or tool is
how you found out about it
how you use it
and explain why you find it better than other methods.

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The tool I rely on most is ...
sentences: The tool I rely on most is Notion, a free app where I keep my study plans, notes and deadlines in one place. I use it almost every day.

steps.label: How I found it
steps.anchor: I first came across it when ...
sentences: A senior at my university recommended it two years ago, when I was struggling to juggle classes and part-time tutoring. At first I found it confusing, so I watched a few short tutorials on YouTube. Within a week I had set up my own pages.

steps.label: How I use it
sentences: Every Sunday, I plan the week with a simple table showing tasks, deadlines and priority levels. I also store lecture notes, copy useful links, and tick off tasks as I finish them. It sends me reminders on my phone, so nothing slips through the cracks.

steps.label: Why it is better
sentences: Before this, I used loose paper notes, and I constantly lost them. This app is user-friendly and works offline, which matters when mobile data is slow. Seeing my progress visually also boosts my motivation.
I also like that I can customise every page to suit my own style of studying.
I would not go back to the old paper method.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: Overall, it has made me noticeably more organised and less anxious.

part3.q: Has technology made people more organised or more distracted?
part3.a: Both, in my opinion. Good apps help people keep track of tasks, but notifications and social media constantly pull attention away. The result depends on self-discipline, and I have seen friends become more distracted than before.

part3.q: Why do some people still prefer paper notebooks to digital tools?
part3.a: Writing by hand feels slower, but it helps many people remember information. Paper also has no notifications or battery problems. My mother, for example, still keeps a diary because she finds a screen tiring and prefers the personal touch.

part3.q: Should schools teach students how to use productivity tools?
part3.a: I think they should, because most students already use phones heavily without a clear method. A short course on planning apps and focus techniques would be practical. It could also warn students about digital clutter and wasted hours.

part3.q: What are the risks of depending too much on technology at work?
part3.a: People can become helpless when systems fail, such as during power cuts or internet outages, which are common here. There are also privacy risks if data is stored online. Over-reliance may weaken skills like memory and handwriting too.

title: Describe an important decision you made about your education or career.
prompts: what the decision was
what choices you had
who or what influenced you
and explain whether you think it was the right decision.

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: One decision that shaped my life was ...
sentences: One decision that shaped my life was choosing to study computer science instead of medicine. I made it in Class Twelve, when I was seventeen.

steps.label: The choices
steps.anchor: At that time, I had to choose between ...
sentences: In my family, medicine is considered the most respectable path, so my parents expected me to sit the medical admission test. My other option was engineering at a public university. I spent weeks weighing up the options, listing pros and cons in a notebook.

steps.label: Influences
sentences: My cousin, who works as a software developer, showed me how he builds apps and earns well from home. I also realised I enjoyed solving logic problems far more than memorising anatomy. My parents were worried, but they agreed to give me a chance.

steps.label: Was it right
sentences: I'm convinced it was the right choice, because I look forward to my classes and have already completed two internships. Job prospects in tech are strong, and I can even freelance. Of course, the first year was tough, and I doubted myself sometimes.
Eventually my mother said that happiness in my work mattered more than status.
I am glad I trusted my own judgement rather than only the family's expectations.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: If I could go back, I would make the same leap again.

part3.q: Should young people choose a career based on passion or salary?
part3.a: Ideally both, but I would put passion first because interest keeps you going through hard years. Salary matters too, especially in a country like ours where families depend on income. The wisest path is to find a field where you can combine the two.

part3.q: How much influence should parents have on a student's choice of subject?
part3.a: Parents should offer guidance, not make the final decision. They have life experience, but they may rely on outdated ideas of what is a good profession. In Bangladesh, family pressure is strong, so open conversation between parents and teenagers is vital.

part3.q: Is it common in your country to change careers in mid-life?
part3.a: It is becoming more common, especially among younger professionals who move from banking to technology or freelancing. But in earlier generations, people stayed in one job for life because of security concerns. Mid-life changes are still seen as risky by many families.

part3.q: Why do some students regret their choice of university course?
part3.a: Often they choose a course because of pressure from family or friends, or because of its reputation, without understanding it. Later they discover that the subject doesn't suit their interests. Better career counselling at school would help avoid this.

phrases.m: a choice that alters your future

title: Describe a river, lake or pond that you have seen and remember well.

what it looks like
what people do there
and explain why it is memorable for you.

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The place I remember best is ...
sentences: The river I remember best is the Meghna, which I crossed by launch during a family trip to Chandpur. It is one of the widest rivers I have ever seen.

steps.label: Where and what it looks like
sentences: It lies in the south-east of Bangladesh, where several big rivers merge before reaching the sea. The water was brownish from the silt, but the surface shone golden at sunrise. The opposite bank was so far away that it felt like an ocean.

steps.label: What people do
sentences: Fishermen were casting nets from small wooden boats, and traders were loading baskets of hilsa onto trucks. Passengers sat on the deck, sipping tea and chatting. Children waved at us from the shore.

steps.label: Why it is memorable
sentences: That morning was the first time I felt how much our country depends on its rivers. The cool breeze and the calm, steady rhythm of the engine made the journey surprisingly peaceful. I still remember the smell of fresh fish and wet mud.
I also remember the loud horn of the launch echoing across the water.
I tell friends that sunrise on a big river is worth the long journey.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: I would love to visit again, perhaps in the rainy season when the river is at its fullest.

part3.q: Why are rivers so important to people in your country?
part3.a: Rivers provide water for farming, fish for food, and routes for transport. Bangladesh is a delta, so most of our land was actually created by river silt. Millions of families, including my own relatives, depend on them for a living.

part3.q: What causes water pollution and how can it be reduced?
part3.a: Factory waste, untreated sewage and plastic rubbish are the main causes. Stricter rules for industries and proper treatment plants would help a great deal. Public awareness is equally important, since many people still throw rubbish directly into the water.

part3.q: Do people in cities have enough contact with natural water bodies?
part3.a: Not really. In big cities like Dhaka, most rivers and canals are polluted or built over, so people have few chances to enjoy them. Creating clean riverside parks would give residents a place to relax and reconnect with nature.

part3.q: Should the government limit building near rivers and lakes?
part3.a: I think they should, at least in flood-prone areas. Illegal construction blocks the natural flow of water and puts families at risk. Strong regulations, along with fair compensation for affected people, would protect both rivers and communities.

title: Describe a time when bad weather changed your plans.

what the weather was like
what you did instead

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: I'd like to tell you about ...

steps.label: The plan
sentences: The whole class had been looking forward to a two-day trip with a bus ride, a beach football match, and a bonfire at night. We had saved pocket money for months. Everyone packed their bags a week before.

steps.label: The weather
sentences: Two days before departure, dark clouds covered the sky and there was a downpour for hours. The weather office announced signal number four for the coast. Our teachers had no choice but to call the trip off.
I was especially excited because it was my first trip without my parents.

steps.label: What we did
sentences: We were disappointed at first, but our class teacher arranged a small party in the school hall. We played cards, sang songs, and shared the snacks we had bought for the journey. Strangely, it became one of our most cheerful memories.
I also learned that plans should always have a backup.

steps.label: Feelings
sentences: Looking back, I was sad but relieved, because the storm turned out to be severe and safety mattered most.

part3.q: Does weather affect people's mood and behaviour?
part3.a: Definitely. Many people feel low and sleepy on grey, rainy days, while sunny weather lifts their energy. In Bangladesh, intense summer heat also makes people irritable and less productive, so I think the climate shapes daily behaviour quite strongly.

part3.q: How has weather in your country changed in recent decades?
part3.a: It has become less predictable. Summers feel hotter, rainfall is more irregular, and floods and cyclones seem more intense than they were in my parents' time. Many farmers say they can no longer rely on traditional seasons.

part3.q: Why do some people pay little attention to weather warnings?
part3.a: Some think warnings are exaggerated because earlier alerts did not result in damage. Others lack information or fear leaving their homes and belongings. In coastal areas, I have seen people stay behind simply because they could not afford to lose their cattle.

part3.q: How can cities prepare better for extreme weather?
part3.a: Cities need better drainage, stronger embankments and reliable early-warning systems sent by phone. Shelters should be well stocked and clearly marked. Regular drills, like those done in coastal schools, would help people react calmly.

phrases.p: at the mercy of the weather

steps.label: How we care for it

Last monsoon, a storm broke one branch, and the whole family felt genuinely sad about it.
My cousins and I even take photos under it every year.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: That is why we would never cut it down, whatever happens.

part3.q: Why do many people enjoy growing plants at home?
part3.a: Many people find gardening relaxing after a stressful day, and it gives a sense of achievement. In cities, where space is limited, balcony plants also bring a little greenery. My mother says looking after her roses calms her mind.

part3.q: Should schools teach children to plant and look after trees?
part3.a: Yes, I think so. Planting a sapling teaches responsibility and patience, and children enjoy watching it grow. Schools could give each class a tree to look after, so students feel proud of it and learn about nature from experience.

part3.q: What are the benefits of having trees in crowded cities?
part3.a: Trees cool the air, absorb pollution, and provide shade in hot weather. They also support birds and give people a place to relax. Dhaka would be much more liveable with more trees, since the summer heat there is overwhelming.

part3.q: Why is cutting down forests still common in many countries?
part3.a: Mostly for money and space. Land is cleared for farms, housing and timber, and the benefits are immediate while the damage appears slowly. Weak law enforcement makes things worse, so countries need stronger protection together with alternative income for local people.

title: Describe an effort made by people in your area to protect the environment.

who organised or took part in it
what changes it brought

steps.label: Opening
