steps.label: The effort
sentences: Local volunteers noticed that the canal behind our market was choked with plastic bags and bottles. They organised a clean-up every Friday morning, collecting rubbish and sorting it for recycling. They also placed bins along the bank.

steps.label: Who took part
sentences: It was a community-led initiative started by a group of university students, but shopkeepers, children and even our local councillor joined. I took part twice, wearing gloves and carrying sacks. It was tiring but surprisingly enjoyable.
Over time, more neighbours joined, and the group even started a small social media page to share photos.

steps.label: Changes
sentences: Within six months, the water looked cleaner and the terrible smell had reduced. Shopkeepers stopped throwing waste into the canal, and some even switched to paper bags. The campaign also helped raise awareness across the area.
My own family now separates waste at home because of it.

steps.label: Success
sentences: I think it was largely successful, although the next step is stronger rules, since volunteers alone cannot solve the problem.

part3.q: Who should take more responsibility for protecting nature, individuals or governments?
part3.a: Both are responsible, but governments hold the greater power. They can make laws, build treatment systems and punish polluters. Individuals still matter, because without public support, rules are ignored. I think the best results come when the two act together.

part3.q: Why do many people know about environmental problems but do nothing?
part3.a: Because the problems seem too big and distant, and daily life already feels hard. Changing habits also takes effort, such as carrying a cloth bag or sorting waste. Many people think, 'Why should I act if others don't?'

part3.q: Can small actions by individuals really make a difference?
part3.a: I believe they can, especially when many people copy them. One person using a reusable bottle changes little, but a whole neighbourhood doing it reduces thousands of plastic items. Small actions also inspire others, as our canal campaign showed.

part3.q: Should companies that pollute pay higher taxes?
part3.a: Yes, I think so. If factories pay for the damage they cause, they will find cleaner methods. The extra tax revenue could fund waste treatment and green projects. Still, rules must be enforced fairly, or companies will simply find loopholes.

phrases.m: plastic thrown away after one use

title: Describe an animal or bird that you often see near your home.

steps.label: Opening

sentences: The bird I see most often near my home is the oriental magpie-robin, which we call doyel in Bangla.
It is small and black and white, and it is also our national bird.

steps.label: Where and when
sentences: I usually see it early in the morning, around six, when I step onto the balcony with my tea.
It sits on the electric wire opposite our flat, or hops around the mango tree in the yard next door.

steps.label: What it does
steps.anchor: What fascinates me is the way it ...
sentences: What fascinates me is how confident it is. It sings a clear, melodic song, flicks its long tail up and down, and chases away much bigger crows from its territory.
In the monsoon it seems even more active, perhaps because there are more insects around.

steps.label: Why I like it
steps.anchor: I feel quite ... about it because ...
sentences: Honestly, I feel quite attached to it. In a crowded city like Dhaka, where concrete is everywhere, hearing real birdsong makes my day feel calmer.
It also reminds me of my grandmother's village house, where doyels woke us up every morning.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: So although it is just a small bird, it connects me with nature. I would really miss its chirping if the trees nearby were ever cut down.

part3.q: Why are some animal species disappearing in many parts of the world?
part3.a: Mostly because their habitat is being destroyed. Forests are cleared for farmland and housing, and wetlands are filled in. In Bangladesh, for example, many bird species have lost the ponds and marshes they used to depend on. Pollution and illegal hunting make the situation even worse.

part3.q: Is it right to keep wild animals in zoos?
part3.a: I think it is acceptable only when zoos work as proper rescue and breeding centres. If they simply keep animals in small cages for entertainment, that is cruel. A good zoo should protect endangered species and educate visitors, like conservation programmes for tigers that have helped numbers recover in some places.

part3.q: How does urban growth affect wildlife?
part3.a: Quite negatively, in most cases. When cities expand, trees are cut and open land disappears, so animals lose both food and shelter. Some species adapt, such as crows or rats, but sensitive ones simply vanish. In Dhaka, the filling of lakes has already pushed many water birds away.

part3.q: Should people be allowed to keep wild birds as pets?
part3.a: I would say no, in general. Wild birds belong in the open, and capturing them often means separating chicks from their parents. Many die during transport as well. A better option is to keep birds that are bred in captivity, or simply to put out water and grain so that wild ones visit your home freely.

phrases.m: area an animal defends as its own
small natural touch in city life
no longer have a place to live

part3.q: Are cities in your country providing enough green spaces?

part3.q: Should land in cities be used for parks or for housing?
part3.a: I think parks should have priority, at least in the densest areas. Housing is certainly needed, but you can build upwards, whereas once green land is lost, it is almost impossible to bring back. A sensible compromise is to protect existing parks by law and require new developments to include open space.

part3.q: How do green spaces affect people's health?
part3.a: They help in many ways. Walking or playing outdoors improves fitness and reduces stress, and clean air from trees is good for people with breathing problems. Even sitting under a tree for ten minutes can lift your mood, as I notice after a tiring day of study.

part3.q: Who should be responsible for maintaining public parks?
part3.a: Mainly local authorities, because they have the budget and the legal power. But citizens should share the responsibility by not littering and by reporting damage. In some places, residents' committees raise small funds to keep the grounds clean, and that works quite well.

part3.q: Why do many people move from villages to big cities?
part3.a: Mostly for jobs and education. Villages have limited work, especially for young people, while cities offer factories, offices, and universities. Many families also believe that city schools and hospitals are better. As a result, migration continues even though the cost of living in the city is high.

part3.q: What are the advantages of living close to nature?
part3.a: There are quite a few. The air is cleaner, life is quieter, and people tend to know their neighbours, so there is less loneliness. Food is often fresher too. I also think the slower pace is good for mental health, which I could feel after even one day in my grandparents' village.

part3.q: Is rural life changing in your country, and how?
part3.a: Yes, it is changing fast. Mobile phones and internet have reached most villages, and many houses now have electricity and brick walls. Farmers use machines and sell crops through mobile banking. The downside is that traditional crafts and community activities are slowly fading.

part3.q: Would it be good for city children to spend time in the countryside regularly?
part3.a: Definitely. City children spend most of their time indoors with screens, so a short stay in the countryside would teach them where food comes from and let them play outside. Schools could organise a yearly village stay, and I believe the children would come back more curious and more grateful.

title: Describe a flood, storm or other natural event that affected people you know.

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The natural event I want to describe is ...
sentences: I would like to talk about the flood that hit Sylhet in the summer of 2022, which badly affected my uncle's family.
Heavy rain in the hills and rising rivers meant that water entered the city within a few hours.

steps.label: What happened
sentences: Their ground floor was under more than a metre of water, and electricity and mobile networks were cut off for several days. Furniture, books and food stocks were ruined.
Worse, clean drinking water was almost impossible to find, and several relatives fell ill with stomach infections.

steps.label: How people coped
sentences: They moved to the first floor of a neighbour's building and shared limited food with other families. Local youth groups arrived in small boats with dry food and water, which was a huge help.
After the water went down, everybody joined in to clean mud from the houses and throw away spoiled things.

steps.label: What could have helped
steps.anchor: In my opinion, the damage could have been reduced if ...
sentences: In my view, much of the damage could have been avoided with better warnings and drainage. Many canals were blocked by rubbish and illegal construction, so water had nowhere to go.
If people had received early alerts on their phones, they could have moved valuables and children to safety.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: Looking back, it showed me how fragile everyday life is. It also made me respect how strongly communities support one another in a crisis.

part3.q: Why are some countries more affected by natural disasters than others?
part3.a: Geography plays a big role. Low-lying, densely populated countries like Bangladesh sit on huge river systems and near the sea, so floods and cyclones are common. Poorer countries also suffer more because they lack strong infrastructure and money for recovery, while richer nations can build barriers and shelters.

part3.q: Is climate change responsible for more frequent extreme weather?
part3.a: I think it is a major factor, though not the only one. Warmer oceans produce stronger cyclones, and melting ice raises sea levels. Scientists link the growing number of heatwaves and heavy rains with global warming. Local problems like deforestation add to the damage, but climate change is the common thread.

part3.q: What role should international organisations play after a disaster?
part3.a: They should mainly provide emergency relief, funding, and technical expertise, since poorer governments often cannot cope alone. After a flood, for instance, they can deliver clean water and medicine quickly. However, they must work with local communities so that the help matches real needs and money is not wasted.

part3.q: How can ordinary people prepare for natural disasters?
part3.a: Several simple things help. Families can keep an emergency bag with dry food, torches, and documents, and learn the nearest shelter location. They should follow weather warnings and store clean water in advance. Even small steps like these can save lives when a storm arrives suddenly.

phrases.m: ability to recover from climate shocks

steps.label: What I changed

sentences: Now I put my phone on charge in another room an hour before bed. I drink a glass of warm milk, read a few pages of a novel, and switch off the lights at eleven sharp.

steps.label: Why and when
steps.anchor: At first, it was hard to ...
sentences: I decided to do this about six months ago, during my exam preparation. I was constantly sleep-deprived, I could not concentrate in class, and I was relying on three or four cups of tea every day.

steps.label: The difficulty
steps.anchor: Since then, I have noticed that ...
sentences: The first two weeks were really difficult. I kept reaching for my phone out of habit, and I often lay awake feeling restless.

steps.label: Effect on me
sentences: The effect has been remarkable. I wake up feeling well-rested, my mood is more stable, and I no longer need tea to get through the morning.
My grades improved a little too, and I feel less irritable with my family.

part3.q: Why do many young people nowadays sleep less than they should?
part3.a: There are a few reasons. Many of them stay up late on social media or watching series, and the content is designed to keep them hooked. Others have heavy study or work schedules. On top of that, they tend to think they can recover on weekends, which does not really work.

part3.q: Should schools and offices start later in the day to help people sleep more?
part3.a: I think a later start would help, especially for teenagers, whose body clock naturally shifts later. Some schools abroad have tried it and reported better concentration. In practice, though, it is hard in places like ours, because of traffic and transport schedules. Flexible office hours might be a more realistic start.

part3.q: How has technology affected the way people sleep?
part3.a: It has had a mostly negative effect. Bright screens delay the production of melatonin, and constant notifications interrupt rest. However, technology can also help, for example through sleep-tracking apps or soothing audio. The key is to use it with discipline rather than letting it control us.

part3.q: Do you think people take sleep as seriously as diet and exercise?
part3.a: Probably not. People talk about diets and gym routines all the time, but sleep is often treated as something to sacrifice when busy. Yet research shows that poor sleep harms the immune system and mental health. I think awareness is slowly growing, but we still have a long way to go.

unable to relax or stay still

title: Describe a traditional home remedy that people in your family use.

steps.label: What it is made of
sentences: It is quite simple. My mother crushes a thumb-sized piece of fresh ginger, boils it with a handful of tulsi leaves from our small garden for ten minutes, then adds a spoonful of honey and a few drops of lemon.
The taste is sharp and slightly spicy, but very comforting.

steps.label: When and who taught us
sentences: We use it at the first sign of a cough or a cold, especially in winter when the temperature drops suddenly. The recipe came from my grandmother, who learned it from her own mother in the village.

steps.label: Does it work
sentences: As for whether it works, I would say it partly does. It soothes the throat and clears the nose, and the warmth helps me sleep. I doubt it can cure serious infections, though.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: To conclude, it is a small tradition that makes me feel looked after, and I plan to teach my own children one day.

part3.q: Why do some people prefer traditional remedies to modern medicine?
part3.a: Many see them as natural and gentle, with fewer side effects than strong medicines. Others simply trust what their parents did, or cannot afford regular doctor visits. In villages, herbal practitioners are also easier to reach than hospitals, so tradition becomes the natural first choice.

part3.q: Should traditional medicine be taught alongside modern medicine?
part3.a: I think it could be introduced as an additional subject, since some traditional treatments have scientific value. Several modern drugs, for example, come from plants. But students must also learn to test claims with evidence, so they can separate useful practices from myths.

part3.q: What are the risks of treating illnesses without seeing a doctor?
part3.a: The biggest risk is delay. A person might use herbs for days while a serious condition, such as typhoid or heart disease, gets worse. Self-medicating with antibiotics is another danger because it causes resistance. A quick check-up is always safer than guessing.

part3.q: How has people's attitude to medicine changed over the generations?
part3.a: It has changed quite a lot. Older people tend to rely on home remedies and trust local healers, while younger people usually search online or go to a clinic first. Better education and access to hospitals have shifted trust to science, although many families still keep a bit of both.

given from one generation to the next

I also learned that fear often exaggerates the difficulty, and that trusting your team makes a big difference.

steps.label: Would I repeat it
sentences: Yes, I would definitely do it again. I am even thinking of joining a weekly session to build stamina, because it is fun and a great full-body workout.

part3.q: Why do some people find it hard to stay active as they get older?
part3.a: Their bodies slow down and joints become stiff, so exercise can feel painful. Many also have long working hours and family duties, leaving little free time. Some worry about injury, or feel embarrassed in a gym full of younger people. Gentle activities like walking can help to overcome these barriers.

part3.q: Should physical education be compulsory in schools?
part3.a: I believe it should be, at least up to a certain age. Many children do not exercise at home, and school may be the only chance to build the habit. However, lessons should be enjoyable and offer choices, otherwise students may start to dislike sport.

part3.q: Is it better to exercise alone or in a group?
part3.a: It depends on the person. Exercising in a group gives motivation and a sense of fun, and you are less likely to skip a session. On the other hand, going alone offers freedom and quiet time. Personally, I prefer a group, since my friends keep me accountable.

part3.q: What can governments do to encourage people to exercise more?
part3.a: They could build more public playgrounds, walking tracks and cycle lanes, and keep them safe and free to use. Campaigns on television and social media can raise awareness. Offering tax benefits for companies that run workplace fitness programmes would also help, as many office workers sit for hours.

phrases.m: a way of life with little movement

title: Describe a meal that was both healthy and delicious.

steps.label: What the meal was

For dessert, we had slices of fresh papaya from our neighbour's tree.

steps.label: Who made it and where
steps.anchor: It was prepared by ... and we ate it ...
sentences: My mother prepared everything at home, and she cooked with very little oil. We ate together around the dining table at about one in the afternoon, after Friday prayers, with the whole family present.

part3.q: Why is junk food so popular among young people?

part3.q: Should unhealthy food be taxed by the government?
part3.a: I think a moderate tax on sugary drinks and fried snacks can work, as it did in a few countries where consumption dropped. But it should be combined with education, and healthy options must be affordable. Otherwise, low-income families would simply pay more without any better choices.

part3.q: Do you think people in your country eat more healthily than in the past?
part3.a: In some ways, yes, as awareness is growing, and more people read food labels and go to gyms. However, in cities, processed snacks and sweet drinks are consumed far more than before. Our grandparents ate mainly home-cooked food and walked a lot, so I would say the overall picture is mixed.

part3.q: How can parents encourage children to develop good eating habits?
part3.a: The best way is to set an example, since children copy what they see. Parents can involve them in cooking, keep fruit within reach, and avoid using sweets as a reward. It also helps to eat together without screens, so mealtime becomes pleasant rather than a battle.

phrases.m: eating a variety of healthy foods

title: Describe a visit to a doctor or clinic that you remember well.

what happened during the visit
how you felt about the care you received
and explain why you still remember this visit.

taking my father for a check-up

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The visit I remember well was when ...
sentences: The visit I remember most clearly was a trip to a government hospital in Dhaka two years ago, when I had a very high fever.

steps.label: Why I went
steps.anchor: The reason I went was that ...
sentences: I had been running a temperature of nearly 40 degrees for three days, with severe body aches and a headache. My mother became worried and took me to the outpatient department.
It was a Sunday morning and the corridor was packed.

steps.label: What happened
sentences: We waited almost two hours with a numbered slip in our hands. When my turn came, the doctor examined me quickly, asked a few questions, and ordered a blood test for dengue.
The result came back positive, so I was admitted for three days and given fluids through a drip.

steps.label: How I felt about the care
steps.anchor: Overall, I felt ... about the care because ...
sentences: The doctor was knowledgeable and surprisingly kind, and the nurses checked on me every few hours. On the other hand, the ward was crowded and the waiting time was long.
Still, I felt well looked after, particularly considering how many patients they had to see.

steps.label: Why I remember it
sentences: I still remember the visit because it was the first time I was seriously ill. It also made me appreciate how hard doctors work, and I now drink plenty of water and avoid mosquito bites very carefully.

part3.q: What problems do hospitals and clinics face in your country?
part3.a: Overcrowding is the biggest one. Public hospitals have too few doctors and beds for the number of patients, so people wait for hours. Rural clinics often lack equipment and specialists. In addition, medicine and tests can be costly for poor families who have to pay out of pocket.

part3.q: Should healthcare be free for everyone?
part3.a: Ideally, yes, because health is a basic right. No one should lose their savings because of an illness. But it requires a large budget and efficient management. A realistic step is to make basic care and emergency treatment free, while charging for non-essential services.

part3.q: Why do some people avoid going to the doctor until they are seriously ill?
part3.a: There are a few reasons. Some fear bad news, and others worry about the cost or cannot take time off work. In villages, the clinic may be far away. People also tend to say it is only a minor thing and wait, which can turn a small problem into a serious one.

part3.q: How might technology change the way people get medical advice in the future?
part3.a: I think online consultations will become common. People will describe symptoms through an app and speak to doctors by video, which will save travel time, particularly in remote areas. Artificial intelligence may also help to screen test results, though a human doctor should always make the final decision.

patient who does not stay overnight
pay medical costs from one's own money

title: Describe a bad habit you gave up for the sake of your health.

how long you had it
what helped you to give it up
and explain how your life is different now.

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The habit I gave up was ...
sentences: The bad habit I gave up was drinking several bottles of fizzy drinks every day, and I did it for the sake of my health.

steps.label: What the habit was
sentences: I had this habit for roughly five years, starting in high school. I used to buy a cold cola with every meal, and during exam time I sometimes finished two big bottles in a day.
Eventually, I gained weight and began to get toothaches.

steps.label: What helped
sentences: What really helped was a check-up at the dentist, who warned me about cavities and the amount of sugar I was consuming. After that, I replaced soft drinks with lemon water and unsweetened tea.
My roommate also supported me, and we made a small bet that whoever gave in first would buy the other lunch.

steps.label: How hard it was
sentences: It was not easy at all. The first week I had strong cravings and a mild headache, and I almost relapsed when friends ordered drinks at a restaurant.
Gradually, though, the urge faded, and I found that plain water tasted fine.

steps.label: Life now
sentences: These days I feel much lighter and more energetic, and I have lost about six kilos. My teeth are healthier, and I save a good amount of money, so I feel proud that I managed to kick the habit.

part3.q: Why is it so difficult for people to break bad habits?
part3.a: Because habits become automatic. They are linked to emotions and routines, so the brain craves the reward even when the person wants to stop. Stress can trigger a relapse too. Without a clear plan and some support, willpower alone often runs out after a few days.

part3.q: Who has more influence on a person's habits, family or friends?
part3.a: I think family has more influence in childhood, since children copy what they see at home, such as eating or sleeping patterns. In the teenage years and later, friends become more powerful, because people want to fit in. So the two matter at different stages of life.

part3.q: Should there be stricter laws against harmful habits like smoking?
part3.a: I believe stricter laws can help, especially banning smoking in public places and selling cigarettes to minors. Higher prices also discourage people. But laws need to be enforced seriously, and combined with campaigns and support for those who want to quit, otherwise the effect will be limited.

part3.q: Do you think people today are more health-conscious than previous generations?
part3.a: I think so, mostly because information is so easy to find. Young people follow fitness trends, count steps, and read about nutrition online. Previous generations had less access to this knowledge. However, stress and unhealthy snacks are everywhere, so being aware does not always mean people actually behave healthily.

phrases.m: stop a bad habit for good
go back to an old habit

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: The moment I remember most clearly is ...

steps.label: Cause
steps.anchor: What made it worse was that ...
sentences: I had three assignments and a presentation due in the same week, and I had put off my thesis for too long.
On top of that, load shedding kept cutting my electricity at night, so I could not study properly.
My parents kept asking if I was fine, but I just said yes.

steps.label: How I felt
sentences: I could not sleep, I skipped meals, and I kept refreshing my phone instead of working.
Honestly, I felt like I was about to burn out, and even small things made me snap at my family.

steps.label: What I did

After that I started taking a short walk every day, listening to music, and breaking my work into small daily tasks.

steps.label: Lesson
sentences: I learned that pressure becomes manageable when you plan ahead and allow yourself to unwind.
Now I start early and never ignore the warning signs.

part3.q: What are the main causes of stress for students and workers today?
part3.a: I think the biggest cause for students is exam competition, especially in Bangladesh where one result can seem to decide your whole future. For workers, long hours, job insecurity and heavy traffic add to the strain. For example, many of my friends spend three hours a day commuting in Dhaka and arrive at work already exhausted. Money worries tie all of this together.

part3.q: Is stress always a bad thing?
part3.a: No, not always. A small amount of stress can keep you alert and push you to prepare properly, like the nervousness before a presentation that makes you rehearse more. The problem starts when it becomes constant and there is no time to recover. So I would say it is helpful in short bursts and harmful when it lasts for months.

part3.q: Should companies and schools do more to protect people's mental health?
part3.a: Yes, I believe they should, because a stressed person cannot perform well anyway. Schools could hire trained counsellors and reduce the focus on memorising for exams. Companies could offer flexible hours and encourage proper breaks. A few private firms in Dhaka already do this, and their staff tend to stay longer and work better.

part3.q: Why is mental health still a difficult subject to talk about in some communities?
part3.a: Many people see it as a sign of weakness or a lack of faith, so they stay silent. In our society, family reputation matters a lot, and people worry about what others will say. For example, someone who is depressed may be told to just pray more or be patient. Until we speak about it openly, many will go without proper help.

sentences: Unlike most young people I know, he does not sit with a phone all day or order fast food.

steps.label: What I learned

sentences: I have learned that staying in good shape is about small habits repeated for years, not extreme diets.

sentences: These days I try to copy his routine when I visit, and I have started walking after dinner.
I hope I can age as gracefully as he has.

part3.q: Why are people living longer than before?
part3.a: I think the main reason is better healthcare and vaccination. Diseases that used to be deadly, such as cholera or tuberculosis, are now treatable. Cleaner water and improved nutrition have also helped. In Bangladesh, life expectancy has risen noticeably in just a few decades, which shows how much difference basic medical access makes.

part3.q: How can elderly people be helped to stay independent?
part3.a: They need affordable healthcare, safe public spaces and a bit of technology to feel confident. For example, ramps and handrails make it easier to move around without help. Community centres where they can meet others also reduce loneliness. Most importantly, we should ask them what they need instead of deciding for them.

part3.q: Should younger family members be responsible for looking after elderly relatives?
part3.a: In our culture, I think yes, to a large extent, because our parents sacrificed a lot for us. Living together also lets children share the load. part3.q: Will the lifestyle of future generations be healthier or less healthy than today's?
part3.a: I am a little pessimistic. Many young people sit all day at screens, eat processed food and sleep too little. On the other hand, there is more awareness about fitness and mental health than before. So I think it depends on whether people actually act on that knowledge, and right now many do not.

It is celebrated all over Bangladesh, but in Dhaka it has a special festive atmosphere.

steps.label: What happens
sentences: Early in the morning, crowds in red and white gather under the banyan tree at Ramna Park to hear traditional songs.
Streets are filled with colourful masks, fairs and food stalls selling panta bhat, hilsa and sweets.
Every year the crowd grows bigger, and the energy is hard to describe.

steps.label: My family
sentences: My family starts the day with a big breakfast of panta bhat with fried fish and green chilli.

steps.label: Why it matters
steps.anchor: The reason it matters so much is that ...
sentences: It matters because it brings people together regardless of religion or class.

sentences: All in all, it is the one day that makes me proud of being Bengali.

part3.q: Why do some traditional festivals become less popular over time?

In big cities, young people often prefer global events like Valentine's Day because they feel modern and trendy. Also, when fewer families live together, there is nobody to organise the preparation. Without that effort, a festival slowly fades.

part3.q: Do festivals bring communities closer together?
part3.a: Yes, I strongly believe so. People who normally do not talk to each other cook, decorate and celebrate together. During Eid, for example, neighbours exchange food and visit each other's homes. These small gestures build trust and a sense of belonging that last long after the holiday.

part3.q: Is it right for festivals to be promoted for tourism?
part3.a: I think it is fine as long as the festival keeps its authenticity. Tourism brings income to local artists and sellers. However, if it becomes too commercial, the meaning may be lost, and locals might feel excluded. So I would support promotion if the community itself benefits and controls it.

part3.q: Should the government spend money on preserving cultural events?
part3.a: Yes, to a reasonable degree, because culture is part of national identity and, once lost, cannot be recovered. Money can fund archives, training for folk performers, and support for community events. But the government should also pay attention to schools and hospitals first. A balance between the two seems the best approach.

part3.q: Why are young people choosing Western-style clothes over traditional ones?

part3.q: Should schools or workplaces require a dress code?
part3.a: I think workplaces may need a basic dress code for professionalism, but schools benefit more from uniforms. part3.q: How does clothing reflect a person's identity?
part3.a: Clothes communicate who we are, from our region and religion to our personality. A person wearing a handloom saree tells you something about their heritage. Others use clothing to express rebellion or creativity. So what we wear is like a silent introduction before we even speak.

part3.q: Can fashion help keep a culture alive?
part3.a: Yes, I think it can. When designers modernise traditional patterns, for example by using Jamdani motifs on jackets, young people become interested again. This also keeps weavers employed, so the skills are not lost. Fashion shows and celebrities wearing local fabrics help too.

Then everyone feeds her sweets, and the same ritual is repeated at the groom's home, with a much smaller crowd.
Everyone takes pictures, and the bride usually ends up bright yellow from head to toe.

steps.label: Who takes part
sentences: Mostly it is the close female relatives and friends, especially cousins who tease the bride and sing songs.
At my cousin's Gaye Holud, even my grandmother joined in, and the whole house was laughing and taking photos.

steps.label: Why interesting
steps.anchor: What I love about it is ...
sentences: I find it interesting because it is not just ritual but also a way for the extended family to bond before the formal wedding.
The yellow colour is said to bring good luck and glowing skin, and it makes everything feel joyful.
It makes a serious event feel relaxed and friendly.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: To sum up, it is a custom full of warmth and humour.
I would love to keep it at my own wedding.

part3.q: How have weddings changed in your country over the past few decades?
part3.a: Weddings have become far bigger and more public. Decades ago, they were mostly held at home with relatives and neighbours. Now many people hire large halls, professional photographers and caterers. Social media has also pushed couples to make events look impressive.

part3.q: Do people spend too much money on weddings?
part3.a: I believe many do, especially for the sake of status. Families sometimes take loans just to impress guests, and then struggle for years afterwards. I would rather see that money used for a house or education. But I understand that weddings are emotional, so people find it hard to hold back.

part3.q: Should couples follow family traditions even if they disagree with them?
part3.a: I think they should respect traditions that matter to elders but have the freedom to drop practices that feel meaningless or costly. Compromise is the key. For example, a couple could keep the main ceremony but skip an expensive reception. That way both generations feel heard.

part3.q: Why do some customs survive for hundreds of years while others disappear?
part3.a: Customs survive when they carry emotional meaning and are fun, like exchanging gifts or singing together. People pass them on because they create memories. Others disappear when they become impractical or are seen as unfair, such as certain dowry practices. So a custom needs both relevance and a positive purpose to last.

part3.q: Do films and dramas influence the way people think about society?

part3.q: Why do some people prefer foreign films to local ones?

part3.q: Should the government control what is shown on television?

part3.q: Can entertainment be a good way to learn about other cultures?

part3.q: Are neighbours as close to each other now as they were in the past?

part3.q: Why do some people prefer to live in a community where everyone knows each other?

part3.q: Should young people be required to do volunteer work?

However, schools could include community service as part of the curriculum, with real projects like tree planting. This builds empathy, and many students continue volunteering by choice afterwards.

part3.q: What can be done to build a stronger sense of community in big cities?
part3.a: Cities could create more shared spaces such as parks, libraries and community halls, where residents meet naturally. Apartment buildings can organise festivals or clean-up days. Neighbourhood groups on social media also help, if they lead to real meetings. Small actions like greeting each other regularly make a big difference.

title: Describe a local craft or art form that is made in your region.
prompts: what it is and how it is made
who makes it
where you first came across it
and explain why it is worth preserving.
angles: Clay pottery from Dhamrai or Rajshahi
Muslin and Jamdani weaving in Narayanganj

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: A craft from my region that I admire is ...
sentences: I want to talk about nakshi kantha, a form of embroidery that is made in rural Bangladesh, especially around Jessore and Mymensingh.
It turns old cloth into beautiful quilts and wall hangings.

steps.label: How it's made
sentences: Women layer old sarees and stitch them together with colourful thread, creating patterns of flowers, birds and village scenes.
A single large piece can take several months, because every stitch is done by hand.
Some designs are inspired by folk tales their grandmothers told them.

steps.label: Who and where
sentences: It is mostly made by village women, often in groups after finishing the housework.
I first saw one at my aunt's house, and later at a craft fair in Dhaka, where I was amazed at the detail.
Seeing the fine stitching, I could not believe it was done without a machine.

steps.label: Why preserve
steps.anchor: I think it is worth saving because ...
sentences: It tells stories of rural life, and it gives women an independent income.
Once those skills are lost, no factory can replicate that personal touch.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: So I think nakshi kantha deserves more support and attention.
I always try to buy it directly from the artisans.

part3.q: Why are traditional crafts disappearing in many places?
part3.a: Mainly because machine-made goods are cheaper and faster. A hand-embroidered quilt takes months and costs a lot, so few buyers can pay for it. Also, young people prefer office jobs to years of training in a craft. As older artisans retire, the knowledge disappears.

part3.q: Should the government support people who work in traditional crafts?
part3.a: Yes, I think they should, because these crafts are part of national heritage. Support could come as training, loans, or help in selling products abroad. For instance, an organised market would let artisans avoid middlemen who take most of the profit. Without help, many would simply give up.

part3.q: Do tourists help or harm local art and crafts?
part3.a: It can be both. On the positive side, tourists buy products and give artists a livelihood. But demand for cheap souvenirs may push makers to rush, copy designs, or lower quality. If visitors show real interest and pay fair prices, they help; if they only bargain hard, the craft suffers.

part3.q: Is machine-made always worse than handmade?
part3.a: Not necessarily. Machines can produce good quality consistently and make products affordable for everyone. But handmade items usually have character, and no two are exactly the same. So I think each has its place, and the value depends on what the buyer wants.

title: Describe a family tradition or rule that has been passed down through generations.
prompts: what the tradition or rule is
how it started, as far as you know
how strictly your family follows it
and explain whether you want to continue it in the future.
angles: Touching the feet of elders for blessings
Gathering at grandparents' village home for Eid

steps.label: Opening
steps.anchor: A tradition in my family is ...
sentences: In my family, we have a rule that everyone eats dinner together on Fridays at my grandparents' house.
It has been followed for as long as I can remember.

steps.label: Origins
sentences: My grandfather says it started when he was young, because his father believed a family that eats together stays together.
Over time it became a deep-rooted habit, and now four generations sit around one long table.
Even the children are expected to arrive on time and help set the table.

steps.label: How strictly
sentences: We follow it very strictly, and even my uncle who works in Chittagong travels back almost every weekend.
Phones are put away, and my grandmother cooks her special beef curry, which nobody dares to miss.
I also like that it gives us a chance to share news and solve small family problems.

steps.label: Future
steps.anchor: In the future, I want to ...
sentences: I definitely want to continue it, although I may adapt it, perhaps once a month if my schedule is busy.
It is where I feel most connected to my family, and I would like my children to experience that.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: In short, it is a simple rule, but it holds our family together.
I am happy to carry it forward.

part3.q: Do traditions become less important as societies modernise?
part3.a: To some extent, yes. Busy schedules and new technology mean people have less time for rituals. Young people also move to cities or abroad, so family gatherings become rare. However, some traditions adapt, like video calls on festival days, so they survive in a different form.

part3.q: Is the role of the family different today from what it was in the past?
part3.a: It has changed a lot. In the past, the family was the main source of financial support, education and social identity. Today, schools, the state and friends play a larger role, and many families are smaller. However, emotional support from family still matters greatly, especially in a country like ours.

part3.q: Should children always obey the rules set by their elders?
part3.a: I think children should respect their elders and listen to their advice, but not obey blindly. Elders have experience, but the world is changing quickly. For example, a parent may have outdated ideas about careers. A healthy approach is open discussion, where both sides explain their reasons.

part3.q: Why do some people feel pressure to follow traditions they do not believe in?
part3.a: Often because of fear of conflict or fear of social judgment. People worry about disappointing parents or being seen as disrespectful. For instance, someone may attend a ritual they find meaningless just to keep peace. Over time this can cause frustration, so families should create space for honest conversations.

title: Describe a time you met someone from a very different culture.
prompts: who the person was and where you met
what differences you noticed between you
what you talked about
and explain what you learned from the experience.
angles: A tourist from Japan visiting Dhaka
A classmate from Europe at university
A colleague from another country on a project

steps.label: Opening
sentences: Last year I met a Japanese tourist named Kenji while I was volunteering at a book fair in Dhaka.
He was visiting Bangladesh for the first time and needed help finding a good place to eat.

steps.label: Differences
sentences: Several differences stood out immediately: he bowed slightly when greeting me and was extremely punctual.
He was also surprised by the noise in Dhaka, while I was amazed that he never raised his voice.
I felt a little nervous at first, worried I might say something wrong.

steps.label: What we talked about
sentences: We shared a long lunch of biryani, and he asked a lot about our festivals, cricket and tea culture.
In return, he explained why Japanese people work long hours and why trains there run exactly on time.
He even tried to say a few Bangla words, which made us both laugh.

steps.label: Lessons
steps.anchor: From this meeting I learned that ...
sentences: I learned that being open-minded makes conversation easy, even if the language is limited.
It also broke my stereotype that people from rich countries are cold or unfriendly.

steps.label: Wrap-up
sentences: We still exchange messages on holidays.
That one afternoon made me more curious about the world.

part3.q: What problems can arise when people from different cultures work together?
part3.a: Differences in communication style cause many problems. In some cultures people are direct, while in others they avoid saying no to keep harmony. This can lead to misunderstandings about deadlines or feedback. Different attitudes to time and hierarchy matter too. Clear communication and patience usually solve most of these issues.

part3.q: Does travelling help people to become more open-minded?
part3.a: Yes, I think it does, as long as the person interacts with locals rather than staying in hotels. Seeing how others live shows that your way is not the only way. After living abroad, my cousin became much more tolerant. Travelling, therefore, can break stereotypes and build understanding.

part3.q: Is it possible for a culture to stay unchanged in a globalised world?
part3.a: I do not think so. Even small villages are influenced by the internet, global brands and migration. Cultures naturally evolve when they meet others, like how pizza and burgers are now part of everyday life in Dhaka. Core values may survive, but the surface will keep changing.

part3.q: Should immigrants be expected to adopt the customs of their new country?
part3.a: I believe they should respect the laws and basic values of the host country, but not be forced to abandon their own identity. Learning the language and local manners helps them integrate. At the same time, they can keep their food, festivals and religion. A society that allows both tends to be richer and more peaceful.
